title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
1. What is the stereocentre?
Locate it in CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list its four substituents.






Check your answer





The CH(OH) carbon bears OH, H, CH₃ and COOH. They are different, so it is a tetrahedral stereocentre.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
2. Does proton loss invert it?
For hydroxide removing the carboxyl OH proton of lactic acid, does that step invert the alcohol-bearing centre?






Check your answer





No. The drawn proton transfer does not change the bonds or spatial arrangement at that centre. It produces lactate and water.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
3. What does oxidation change?
Oxidise lactic acid’s secondary alcohol to a ketone. Is the original centre still R/S?






Check your answer





The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The former centre is trigonal planar, so it is not assigned R/S.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
4. Which mechanism returns C=O?
Compare an aldehyde addition product with an acyl substitution product.






Check your answer





Addition opens the carbonyl pi bond and produces a tetrahedral product after appropriate protonation. Acyl substitution first adds, then eliminates a viable leaving group to reform C=O.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
section: 5. What does a large mass prove?
text:
5. What does a large mass prove?
A plausible high isolated yield conflicts with major unexpected NMR signals. Which observation should be ignored?






Check your answer





Neither. The apparent yield depends on the identity/purity assumption, while unexpected NMR signals call that assumption into question. Investigate the discrepancy before claiming pure product.

title: Self-check: transfer the reasoning
text:
6. What makes a conclusion inspectable?
Give the ingredients of an evidence-based conclusion and a reproducible report.






Check your answer





State a chemical claim, observations, a reason connecting them, a limitation and a next test. Save raw inputs and code so a fresh R session can recreate tables and plots; separately check chemical validity.



Return to the practice and worked examples for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
text: Allow 90–120 minutes. Work independently, compare explanations in pairs and then inspect the checks. Use drawings, words and quantitative evidence together.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
text:
Case 1. One molecule, several transformations
Lactic acid is CH₃CH(OH)COOH. It is encountered in biological contexts, but this case requires only its drawn functional groups.

Identify its alcohol type, acid group and stereocentre.
Draw hydroxide deprotonation of its carboxyl group with two arrows.
Draw the product of oxidising the secondary alcohol to a ketone.
Draw the target ester made from its acid group and ethanol.
For each change, state whether it changes bonding at the original stereocentre and whether that centre still qualifies for R/S assignment.







Hint





Draw every relevant oxygen and hydrogen. Ask whether the central carbon has four different substituents and remains tetrahedral after the transformation.









Worked comparison





The alcohol is secondary and the CH(OH) carbon is the stereocentre. Hydroxide gives CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻ and water without changing the centre’s bonds. Oxidation gives CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid; the former centre is now planar and is not R/S. Esterification at the acid gives CH₃CH(OH)COOCH₂CH₃ plus water as a net equilibrium transformation; the alcohol-bearing centre remains tetrahedral. These drawings specify target changes, not a promise of perfect selectivity under all conditions. Ordinary proton transfer at the carboxyl OH alone does not invert the stereocentre.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
section: Case 2. Configuration is not a drawing direction
text:
Case 2. Configuration is not a drawing direction
Draw both configurations of lactic acid with one wedged and one dashed bond. Assign priorities OH > COOH > CH₃ > H, explain the COOH/CH₃ tie-break and assign R or S for your own drawings. Redraw one molecule after rotating the whole drawing; verify that the configuration stays the same. Can you infer the sign of optical rotation from that R/S label?






Worked reasoning





O outranks C, and H is lowest. For the two carbon substituents compare their next attached atoms: the acid carbon is treated as attached to O,O,O in CIP multiple-bond bookkeeping, while methyl carbon is attached to H,H,H. Orient the lowest-priority group away; 1→2→3 clockwise is R and anticlockwise is S. If the lowest-priority group points toward you, reverse the apparent result. Rigid rotation preserves configuration. R/S does not determine the sign or size of measured optical rotation.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
section: Case 3. Resolve an unknown with several observations
text:
Case 3. Resolve an unknown with several observations
An unknown has C₄H₈O₂; its complete simulated IR has C=O but no broad O–H. Its simulated proton NMR has 1.25 ppm triplet (3H), 2.05 ppm singlet (3H) and 4.12 ppm quartet (2H). Compare ethyl ethanoate, butanoic acid and a hydroxyketone. For each candidate make at least one testable prediction; then explain which candidate best fits the supplied set.






Worked interpretation





Ethyl ethanoate fits an ester carbonyl, O–CH₂ quartet/CH₃ triplet and acetyl CH₃ singlet. Butanoic acid predicts a broad acid O–H feature and lacks O–CH₂; a hydroxyketone predicts OH and needs a different proton arrangement. These comparisons support the ester candidate among this set. Explicit assignments are stronger than stating that the spectrum “looks like an ester”.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
section: Case 4. Critique a tempting success claim
text:
Case 4. Critique a tempting success claim
For the aspirin teaching reaction, theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. A student reports 1.70 g isolate, a single TLC spot and concludes “pure product, 94% yield”. Their IR has an unexpected feature and NMR has an extra major set of signals. Which numerical statement follows from the mass? Which chemical claim is unsupported? Suggest two possible explanations and a useful next check. Do not diagnose a unique impurity from these limited facts.






Worked critique





The apparent mass-based isolated yield is 100 × 1.70/1.8016 ≈ 94.4%, assuming the isolated mass is product. Purity is unsupported. Residual solvent or a co-migrating organic impurity are possible explanations; incomplete reaction or mistaken assignment is also possible. Compare the full NMR integration and signals against the expected product and appropriate references, or repeat TLC under a suitable different separation condition. The best next check depends on which contradictory feature can be tested most directly.

title: Integrated chemistry workshop
section: Case 5. A report someone else can inspect
text:
Case 5. A report someone else can inspect
Use your own Rmd project to write a short conclusion for a teaching dataset. Include the chemical claim, two observations, the reasoning linking them, one limitation and a proposed next observation. Reopen the project in a fresh R session and Knit from the saved inputs. Ask a partner to find the raw values, the calculation and the evidence supporting each sentence.






Review checklist





The report should reconstruct its own objects, use relative paths and identify the data as simulated when appropriate. The conclusion must distinguish isolated yield, identity and purity and avoid treating a candidate’s filename as evidence. Reproducibility and chemical validity are separate requirements: both must be checked. See practical reporting.



Optional further reading is selected biological examples from Solomons chapters 22–24, through the reading guide. Detailed metabolic pathways and advanced synthesis are outside this workshop.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Plan a short route using known functional-group changes.
Calculate limiting reagent, theoretical amount and isolated yield with units.
Evaluate identity and purity separately from the recovered mass.


Start with a drawn molecule and an explanation from the preceding unit. Ask students to predict before revealing an answer. Use the practice page for complete worked checks rather than putting dense paragraphs on slides.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Plan with functional groups

Oxidation followed by esterification connects ethanol, ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate.Choose a target transformation before selecting conditions.

The route uses a separate ethanol portion in the esterification stage. Strong oxidation to the acid requires suitable conditions; controlled aldehyde isolation is a different objective. These are planning examples, not laboratory instructions.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Balance before calculating

The aspirin teaching example uses one salicylic acid and one acetic anhydride per aspirin.The other product is ethanoic acid; do not drop atoms from the equation.

The sample masses and yields are simulated. The acetylation changes the phenolic OH into an ester while retaining the salicylic-acid carboxyl group.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Find the limiting reagent

10.0 mmol/1 is less than 15.0 mmol/1, so salicylic acid limits theoretical aspirin.Compare n divided by its stoichiometric coefficient, not the masses.

The smaller mass need not be limiting. A change in stoichiometry would change the comparison even if the measured amounts stayed the same.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Predict the maximum product mass

0.0100 mol times 180.16 g/mol gives 1.8016 g theoretical aspirin.Keep units visible and round the final reported result appropriately.

The word theoretical describes the stoichiometric upper bound under assumed complete conversion and no competing pathways. It is not a guarantee of product formation.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Calculate isolated yield

An isolated mass of 1.20 g corresponds to 66.6% of the theoretical mass.A mass-based yield assumes that the weighed material is the stated product.

Residual solvent, water or impurities can inflate the apparent mass. Do not call this conversion, and do not claim purity solely from a plausible percentage.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Read a TLC comparison

The simulated crude lane has spots matching starting-material and product references under the same conditions.A reference match supports a comparison, not unique identification.

The plate is a schematic of supplied teaching observations. TLC retention depends on stationary phase, eluent and conditions; Rf is not a compound-specific constant.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Measure from the origin

For a 3.2 cm spot and 5.0 cm solvent-front travel, Rf = 0.64.Both distances start at the same baseline; the ratio has no units.

Measure the spot centre consistently. If the solvent front is unknown or runs off the plate, an Rf cannot be reliably reconstructed from this drawing.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Ask which functional groups remain

An aspirin-like teaching trace retains acid features and adds ester evidence.Check the expected product structure rather than assuming every starting-material feature should disappear.

The carboxylic acid remains after phenolic acetylation. Do not interpret persistent acid O–H as automatic proof of unreacted salicylic acid; the phenolic and acid OH regions require care.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
section: One spot need not mean one compound
text:
One spot need not mean one compound

Two distinct compounds can have the same Rf in one eluent.Complement TLC with spectral evidence and other suitable purity checks.

Co-migration is a counterexample to the inference “one spot proves pure”. A mixture can also contain components invisible under the chosen detection method.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Keep the calculation reproducible

Saved raw mass and an amount table feed an Rmd calculation and report.Changing an input and knitting again should update every dependent result.

Students should keep raw observations separate from derived columns. Rerendering does not validate whether the raw record or the chemical model is correct; each also needs checking.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
Work one example on paper
Using 1.3812 g salicylic acid (138.12 g/mol) and 1.53135 g acetic anhydride (102.09 g/mol), calculate both amounts, theoretical aspirin mass and yield from 1.20 g isolated material. Explain why these numbers cannot establish purity.

Allow independent thinking, then compare in pairs. Ask students to defend each atom, charge or assignment. Show the worked check only after a first attempt.

title: Synthesis, yield and experimental evidence
text:
A common mistake to repair
“66.6% yield” and “66.6% pure” answer different questions. Also distinguish isolated yield from starting-material conversion and product selectivity.
Explain the correction using a drawing or a specific observation.

text:

Which atoms, bonds or observations support the claim?
What alternative would make a different prediction?
What assumption limits the conclusion?

Give a partner your explanation without the answer label. Can they follow it?

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
1. What does C₄H₈O₂ imply?
Calculate degree of unsaturation for an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule and state one limitation.






Check your answer





(2×4+2−8)/2 = 1. A carbonyl, another double bond or a ring could account for it; formula alone does not establish an ester.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
2. Which IR direction means absorption?
In a transmittance plot, do stronger absorptions point up or down?






Check your answer





They are dips to lower transmittance. An absorbance plot uses a different ordinate. Always inspect the axis label.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
text:
3. Which part of an ethyl group is a quartet?
For O–CH₂–CH₃ in the simple first-order model, give the two multiplicities and integrations.






Check your answer





CH₂ is a quartet integrating to 2H because it sees three adjacent equivalent H. CH₃ is a triplet integrating to 3H because it sees two adjacent H.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
section: 4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
text:
4. Why is acetyl methyl a singlet?
In CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃, explain the 3H signal near 2 ppm using neighbouring atoms.






Check your answer





The carbonyl carbon directly adjacent to that methyl has no H. The distant O–CH₂ hydrogens are not vicinal neighbours of the acetyl methyl in this introductory splitting model.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
5. Can NMR height replace integral?
A schematic triplet is taller than a singlet. Can you conclude that the triplet represents more H?






Check your answer





No. Integral is area over the whole signal, not the tallest line. Use supplied integration or measured integrated area; schematic heights are not quantitative proton counts.

title: Self-check: structure from spectra
text:
6. What rejects the acid candidate?
State two observations in U1 supporting ethyl ethanoate over butanoic acid.






Check your answer





No evident broad acid O–H in a suitable complete IR trace, and a 2H O–CH₂ quartet with matching terminal CH₃ triplet. The acetyl CH₃ singlet supplies additional support.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
text: Allow 60 minutes for structure work and 45 minutes for the R plot. All spectra and peak tables supplied here are simulated teaching examples, not measured spectra. Values are illustrative, and simple splitting uses a first-order model.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
section: 1. Use the formula before looking at a spectrum
text:
1. Use the formula before looking at a spectrum
Unknown U1 has formula C₄H₈O₂. For this ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule, the degree of unsaturation is (2*C + 2 - H)/2. Calculate it. Draw ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid, showing that both satisfy the formula.






Worked check





The degree is (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1. A carbonyl supplies one double bond in either candidate. The formula alone does not decide whether the oxygens are arranged as an ester or a carboxylic acid; it also does not rule out every other possible connectivity. These are two candidate structures to test.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
text:
2. Read the supplied evidence
U1 has strong IR absorption in the ester carbonyl region near 1740 cm⁻¹ and no evident broad acid/alcohol O–H band in the supplied complete trace. Its proton NMR peaks are:

The proton-decoupled carbon NMR shows four signals at approximately 14, 21, 60 and 171 ppm. Assign every supplied observation to ethyl ethanoate. Explain the quartet/triplet relationship and the acetyl methyl singlet.






Hint





First find an O–CH₂–CH₃ fragment. The CH₂ sees three equivalent neighbouring H; the CH₃ sees two. Then account for the remaining three protons.









Worked assignment





For CH₃COOCH₂CH₃: terminal ethyl CH₃ gives 1.25 ppm, triplet, 3H; O–CH₂ gives 4.12 ppm, quartet, 2H; acetyl CH₃ gives 2.05 ppm, singlet, 3H because the adjacent carbonyl carbon has no H. The carbon signals correspond respectively to terminal ethyl CH₃ (14), acetyl CH₃ (21), O–CH₂ (60) and C=O (171). Strong carbonyl IR and no broad O–H agree with the ester. Peak heights in a schematic NMR drawing are not the integrals; use the supplied areas/integral values.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
text:
3. Try to reject the alternative
Explain two independent disagreements between butanoic acid and U1. What would make an argument from an absent IR feature less reliable? Why is the name of a supplied data file not evidence for chemical identity?






Worked reasoning





Butanoic acid would have an acid O–H region and no O–CH₂ quartet. It also would not give the isolated acetyl methyl singlet of the ester. Absence is less informative if the relevant region was not measured, the sample is too dilute, or the signal is obscured. A filename is a label supplied by a person and can be wrong; identity should be tested against the observations.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
section: 4. R task: present an IR comparison
text:
4. R task: present an IR comparison
Open the student project. The supplied data/ir.csv contains sample_id, wavenumber_cm1 and transmittance_percent. Plot the simulated ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid traces. Keep their sample labels so the plotted evidence can be traced back to the data.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ir <- read_csv("data/ir.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
comparison <- ir |>
  filter(sample_id %in% c("ethyl_ethanoate", "ethanoic_acid"))
ggplot(comparison,
       aes(wavenumber_cm1, transmittance_percent, colour = sample_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Wavenumber (cm−1)", y = "Transmittance (%)",
       colour = "Simulated sample") +
  theme_minimal()
Add a report caption explaining that these are simulated traces, that dips indicate absorption in a transmittance plot, and which region distinguishes the candidates. Use a descending wavenumber axis; it is conventional here and does not reverse the underlying physics. Check that transmittance values lie between 0 and 100. Do not fit a model or ask R to assign the unknown for you.






Interpretation check





The acid trace includes a very broad O–H region, while the ester trace lacks that broad feature. Both contain carbonyl absorption. The chemical comparison uses the functional groups expected from the candidate structures; the plot is a way to inspect and communicate the supplied observations. An exact carbonyl position is not a unique molecular fingerprint.

title: A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence
text:
Leave with
A fully annotated structure, a rejected alternative, and a knitted Rmd section with a labelled IR comparison. Read selected Solomons chapters 2 and 9 through the reading guide.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Locate nitrogen lone pairs and predict simple protonation states.
Recognise a simple aromatic pi system and explain contrasting nitrogen sites.
Draw the main charge forms of a simple amino acid at supplied pH values.


Start with a drawn molecule and an explanation from the preceding unit. Ask students to predict before revealing an answer. Use the practice page for complete worked checks rather than putting dense paragraphs on slides.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Name the nitrogen environment

Primary, secondary and tertiary amines have one, two and three carbon substituents on nitrogen.A neutral ordinary amine has three bonds and one lone pair.

The classification counts carbon substituents, not how many hydrogen bonds the molecule can form. Tertiary amines are not automatically positively charged; four-bonded ordinary ammonium nitrogens are.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Protonation uses the lone pair

Methylamine forms methylammonium by donating its nitrogen pair to H+.Four single bonds on nitrogen give a positive formal charge.

Separate H+ as shorthand from the actual proton donor in solution. Students should be able to redraw water or an acid as donor and include the accompanying bond-cleavage arrow.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Amine is not amide

An amide nitrogen lone pair interacts with a neighbouring carbonyl.Do not assign the basicity of a simple alkylamine to peptide nitrogen.

The diagram deliberately compares local structure rather than making an absolute basicity rule for all substituted molecules. Solvent and other substituents matter. Ordinary amide protonation is often preferred at oxygen under strong acid.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: An aromatic ring can change basicity
text:
An aromatic ring can change basicity

Aniline can delocalise its nitrogen lone pair into its benzene ring.Under comparable aqueous conditions aniline is less basic than a simple alkylamine.

The dashed connector indicates orbital participation, not a reaction arrow. If asking for a complete resonance contributor, require the accompanying ring pi-bond shifts and resulting charges. The free base is stabilised by conjugation, affecting its protonation equilibrium.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Aromaticity requires a continuous pi system
text:
Aromaticity requires a continuous pi system

Benzene has six pi electrons in a planar, cyclic, conjugated system.For these simple rings use the 4n + 2 rule only after checking the structural requirements.

The vertical strokes illustrate p-orbital availability schematically, not extra sigma bonds or actual orbital shapes. Six pi electrons occupy the delocalised network; there are not six localised electron pairs.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
A ring is not enough

Benzene is aromatic; cyclohexane lacks the required continuous pi network.Identify the orbitals before counting electrons.

Cyclohexane is not antiaromatic: it is nonaromatic because it lacks continuous conjugation. Detailed antiaromatic cases are outside this lesson.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Pyridine nitrogen keeps a separate lone pair
text:
Pyridine nitrogen keeps a separate lone pair

Pyridine nitrogen supplies one electron to the pi system; its lone pair lies outside that system.Protonation of this lone pair can retain the aromatic sextet.

The aromatic circle represents six delocalised pi electrons. Do not count the displayed lone pair again as part of that six.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: Pyrrole nitrogen supplies a pair to the ring
text:
Pyrrole nitrogen supplies a pair to the ring

Pyrrole has four pi electrons from carbon double bonds plus two from the nitrogen pair.That pair is much less available for ordinary N protonation than the pyridine pair.

Keep pyrrole and pyridine chemically distinct. The dashed connector indicates participation in the delocalised system; it is not a reaction arrow. Pyrrole is a much weaker base at N.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
section: An amino acid can carry two formal charges
text:
An amino acid can carry two formal charges

Glycine changes from net +1 through a zwitterion to net −1 as pH rises.Net neutrality does not mean every atom is uncharged.

Use supplied pKa values near 2.3 for COOH and 9.6 for ammonium if a numerical example is needed. Species coexist around each pKa; the three drawings show dominant forms in well-separated pH regions.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Use conjugate-acid pKa consistently

Ethylammonium has approximate aqueous pKa 10.7; anilinium about 4.6.The larger conjugate-acid pKa corresponds to the stronger base in this comparison.

These are approximate teaching values, not universal solvent-independent constants. Basicity is an equilibrium property; nucleophilicity concerns reaction rate at an electrophile and cannot be ranked solely from this table.

title: Amines and aromatic molecules
text:
Work one example on paper
Draw glycine at pH 1, 6 and 12 using supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6. Mark every formal charge and give the net charge. Explain why the pH 6 drawing is a zwitterion.

Allow independent thinking, then compare in pairs. Ask students to defend each atom, charge or assignment. Show the worked check only after a first attempt.

“Contains nitrogen” is insufficient to predict basicity. Identify the available pair and whether it participates in conjugation or aromaticity.
Explain the correction using a drawing or a specific observation.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
1. What is the attacked atom?
In ethyl ethanoate reacting with hydroxide, identify the initial attacked atom and the electron pair that moves at the same time.






Check your answer





The nucleophile attacks acyl carbon. The C=O pi pair moves onto carbonyl oxygen. Directly attaching OH while retaining every carbonyl bond would give five bonds at carbon.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
text:
2. What is the intermediate charge?
Write the intermediate from OH⁻ addition to CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and locate its negative charge.






Check your answer





CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₂CH₃), net −1. Incoming hydroxide becomes a neutral OH substituent; original carbonyl O now carries the charge.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 3. What is the final acid/base pair?
text:
3. What is the final acid/base pair?
After collapse in basic ester hydrolysis, can carboxylic acid and ethoxide be treated as the final predominant products?






Check your answer





No. Ethoxide deprotonates the much stronger acid to give carboxylate and ethanol. Acid work-up can later protonate the carboxylate.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
text:
4. Does acid plus amine directly give amide?
Predict the initial predominant reaction between ethanoic acid and methylamine in water.






Check your answer





Proton transfer gives ethanoate and methylammonium. Suitable activation or conditions are needed to form an amide; simply losing OH⁻ from the unactivated acid is not an adequate mechanism.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
text:
5. Why is the amide C–N bond less freely rotating?
Connect amide resonance to its geometry without treating resonance contributors as separate molecules.






Check your answer





Nitrogen pair donation into the carbonyl gives partial C–N double-bond character. The charge-separated contributor has O− and N+; both contributors describe one delocalised amide.

title: Self-check: acyl addition and elimination
section: 6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
text:
6. Can an aldehyde follow exactly the same substitution?
Why is a tetrahedral aldehyde intermediate not normally converted to an acyl-substitution product by ejecting its carbon-bound hydrogen?






Check your answer





That would require loss of hydride, a very poor leaving group in this setting. Aldehydes normally undergo carbonyl addition rather than this acyl-substitution analogy.



Return to the practice and worked examples for any reasoning you could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
text: Allow 75–90 minutes. You need carbonyl addition, acid–base arrows and formal charges. Work on paper first; use the figures to check your bond bookkeeping.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
text:
1. Find the acyl carbon
Draw CH₃COOH, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃CONH₂ and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃. Circle any carbonyl carbon. Identify the acid, ester, amide and ether. Explain why an ester oxygen is part of a different reactive motif from an ether oxygen.






Hint





In the condensed formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, the second carbon is C(=O), not a carbon with two unrelated single-bonded oxygens. Redraw the bonds explicitly.









Worked check





The first three structures contain CH₃–C(=O)–Y with Y = OH, OCH₂CH₃ or NH₂. They are acid, ester and amide. The ether contains no carbonyl and no acyl carbon. The ester can undergo attack at carbonyl carbon followed by leaving-group loss; the same carbonyl addition step is unavailable to the ether.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
section: 2. Draw hydroxide addition to an ester
text:
2. Draw hydroxide addition to an ester
Use ethyl ethanoate, CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃. Draw a lone pair from hydroxide oxygen to the acyl carbon and move the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen. Draw the resulting tetrahedral intermediate with every relevant hydrogen and charge. Label the original carbonyl oxygen, incoming oxygen and original ester oxygen.






Worked check





The intermediate is CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₂CH₃). The original carbonyl O is O⁻; the incoming hydroxide oxygen now has C–O and O–H bonds and is neutral. The ethoxy oxygen remains neutral with two bonds. Carbon has four single bonds, and the net charge remains −1. An intermediate retaining C=O as well as both new and old substituents would give five bonds at carbon and is invalid.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
section: 3. Finish the hydrolysis and account for the proton
text:
3. Finish the hydrolysis and account for the proton
Collapse that intermediate by reforming C=O and breaking the acyl C–OEt bond. Then show the acid–base step between the initially formed carboxylic acid and ethoxide. What species predominates in the basic reaction mixture? What does acid work-up change?






Hint





An ordinary carboxylic acid is much more acidic than ethanol. Do not stop at an acid and a strongly basic alkoxide coexisting as the final pair.









Worked check





The O⁻ pair forms a C=O pi bond while the C–OEt pair moves onto ethoxy oxygen. This gives CH₃COOH and CH₃CH₂O⁻ in the simple stepwise model. Ethoxide removes the acid proton to give CH₃COO⁻ and ethanol. Overall, ester plus hydroxide gives carboxylate plus alcohol. Acid work-up protonates carboxylate to the neutral acid; it does not reverse the atom identities in the product. These are mechanistic reasoning drawings, not instructions to conduct a reaction.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
section: 4. Compare aldehyde addition with ester substitution
text:
4. Compare aldehyde addition with ester substitution
Draw hydroxide addition to ethanal as a reversible elementary step. Compare its tetrahedral species with the ester intermediate above. Why is expelling H⁻ from the ethanal intermediate not a reasonable analogy to loss of ethoxide?






Worked check





The aldehyde has H where an ester has OR. Hydride would be an extremely poor leaving group in this setting. An aldehyde can return to its starting carbonyl by reversing addition or proceed through appropriate addition chemistry; it does not ordinarily substitute away its carbon-bound H by this analogy. Product prediction must consider leaving-group viability, not just valence.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
text:
5. Explain an amide using resonance
Draw neutral ethanamide and its charge-separated contributor with a C=N bond. Assign O and N charges and count the total charge. Explain why the C–N bond rotates less freely than a simple amine C–N bond. Then predict the initial outcome of mixing ethanoic acid with methylamine in water.






Worked check





The second contributor is CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. Net charge stays zero, and the actual amide has partial C–N double-bond character. Its nitrogen pair is less available for ordinary protonation than a simple amine pair. Acid plus methylamine initially gives ethanoate and methylammonium; amide formation requires appropriate activation or conditions. This is also why peptide formation in water needs more than simply bringing amino acids together.

title: Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate
text:
Leave with
A complete ester-hydrolysis mechanism, a comparison with carbonyl addition, and an explanation of amide properties. Optional reading is selected Solomons chapter 17; consult the reading guide.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Explain why carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
Follow addition and proton-transfer steps.
Recognise a hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal.


Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: The carbonyl is polar and planar
text:
The carbonyl is polar and planar

Ethanal has an oxygen-polarised carbonyl and approximately trigonal planar geometry at its carbonyl carbon.C=O polarity makes carbon electron-poor. Its π pair can move to oxygen when a nucleophile adds.

Partial charges are not formal charges. The neutral starting carbonyl has no formal positive carbon even though the carbon is electrophilic.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Addition changes carbon geometry

Hydroxide adds to ethanal, giving a tetrahedral intermediate with alkoxide oxygen and a newly attached OH.Two coupled arrows form C–O and move the C=O π pair to oxygen. The total charge remains −1.

The carbon has four single bonds after addition. The original carbonyl oxygen bears the negative charge. Check atom identity rather than treating both oxygens as interchangeable.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Proton transfer completes the hydrate

Water transfers a proton to the alkoxide, giving a geminal diol and regenerating hydroxide.The net reaction is carbonyl + water ⇌ hydrate. The base participates in the pathway and is regenerated.

Not every carbonyl is mostly hydrated at equilibrium. Substituents and conditions affect the equilibrium; mechanism and product proportion are different questions.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Acid can activate the oxygen first
text:
Acid can activate the oxygen first

A carbonyl oxygen lone pair accepts a proton from hydronium, producing protonated carbonyl and water.Protonating oxygen increases carbonyl electrophilicity. Neutral water or alcohol can then be the attacking nucleophile.

Avoid drawing a strongly basic nucleophile freely coexisting in excess strong acid. For this route use neutral nucleophiles and explicit proton transfers.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: An alcohol oxygen supplies a pair
text:
An alcohol oxygen supplies a pair

Methanol attacks the protonated carbonyl; the pi pair moves to oxygen, and the incoming methanol oxygen becomes oxonium.The new tetrahedral species has OH and O⁺HCH₃ attached to the same carbon.

An incoming neutral oxygen changes from two to three bonds and acquires positive charge. The formerly protonated carbonyl oxygen becomes neutral OH after its pi pair returns.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Deprotonate the incoming oxygen

Water accepts a proton from the methoxy oxonium group, forming a neutral hemiacetal and hydronium.A hemiacetal has OH and OR attached to the same carbon. The acid catalyst is regenerated.

Do not remove the proton from the wrong atom without considering the resulting structure. Ask students to label original carbonyl oxygen and incoming alcohol oxygen.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
One substitution changes the class

A hemiacetal carbon has one OH and one OR group; an acetal carbon has two OR groups.A second alcohol can ultimately give an acetal under acid catalysis, with water formed. Additional steps are required.

The left/right diagrams compare product classes; they do not represent a single elementary OH-to-OR substitution. Students are required to understand the hemiacetal steps first.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Conditions control the equilibrium mixture

The acetal equilibrium can be shifted toward acetal by removing water or toward hydrolysis using excess water under acid catalysis.Acid speeds both directions. Changing composition can shift the equilibrium mixture; catalysis alone does not change K.

This is a composition argument, not an experimental recipe. Do not describe an equilibrium arrow as proof of equal concentrations.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: An internal OH can close a ring
text:
An internal OH can close a ring

The terminal alcohol of 5-hydroxypentanal can add to its aldehyde to form a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal.Intramolecular addition conserves the molecular formula. The ring includes the attacking oxygen and the original carbonyl carbon.

Count the six ring atoms: oxygen plus five carbons. This provides a chemical bridge to sugar rings without assuming carbohydrate biochemistry.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: Ask what else is bonded to carbonyl carbon
text:
Ask what else is bonded to carbonyl carbon

An aldehyde bears H at its carbonyl carbon, while an ester bears OR that can participate in an addition–elimination pathway.Aldehydes and ketones ordinarily retain their H/carbon substituents during addition. Acyl derivatives introduce leaving-group chemistry next.

Do not imply that alkoxide departs freely from every tetrahedral intermediate. Protonation state, leaving-group ability and conditions determine the viable pathway.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Same pattern, different nucleophiles
Water gives a hydrate; an alcohol can give a hemiacetal; a hydride equivalent gives an alcohol after proton donation.
Locate the new bond in each product. Keep reagent scope and conditions explicit.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
section: A mechanism and an equilibrium answer different questions
text:
A mechanism and an equilibrium answer different questions
The mechanism accounts for the path and intermediates. The equilibrium describes the relative amounts of species under stated conditions.
Drawing an accessible hydrate does not prove it is the major species.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls
text:
Account for each oxygen
Start with CH₃CHO and CH₃OH. Label the aldehyde oxygen A and alcohol oxygen B.
In the hemiacetal, which is OH and which is OCH₃? What would be wrong with exchanging their atom labels without an extra process?

text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
text:
1. What does propan-2-ol give on selected oxidation?
Retain the carbon skeleton.






Check your answer





Propanone. The carbon bearing OH becomes a carbonyl carbon, while its two carbon substituents remain attached.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
text:
2. Why is a tertiary alcohol a boundary case?
Explain the missing bond at the carbon bearing OH.






Check your answer





It has no C–H bond at that carbon. Simple conversion to C=O while retaining all three C–C bonds would overbond carbon. Harsh oxidation can involve C–C cleavage, outside this selected pattern.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
text:
3. What comes immediately after hydride-equivalent addition?
A ketone receives H at carbon while its pi pair moves to oxygen. Name the species type before work-up.






Check your answer





An alkoxide. A subsequent proton transfer from an explicit donor produces the alcohol. Free hydride in water is not what the simplified H: minus drawing represents.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
text:
4. Does an OH band prove which alcohol is present?
State a limitation of functional-group IR evidence.






Check your answer





No. Many compounds share that functional group, bands can overlap, and samples can contain water or mixtures. Combine multiple observations with structural and purity evidence.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
section: 5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
text:
5. Which amount limits a one-to-one reaction?
Reactants are available as 10.0 and 15.0 mmol. Product coefficient is one.






Check your answer





The 10.0 mmol reactant limits product to 10.0 mmol. Compare amount divided by stoichiometric coefficient, rather than raw masses.

title: Self-check: Alcohols and redox
text:
6. Does 66.6% isolated yield mean 66.6% conversion?
Explain one possible reason they differ.






Check your answer





No. Starting material may react but product may be lost during isolation; side products or impurities can also affect the relationship. Conversion, isolated yield and purity answer different questions.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
text: Allow 60–75 minutes for chemistry problems and 45 minutes for the R calculation. The R task uses the course’s synthesis teaching data as preparation for later reporting. That dataset describes aspirin formation, not an alcohol oxidation.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
section: 1. Keep track of the changing carbon
text:
1. Keep track of the changing carbon
Draw ethanol, ethanal and ethanoic acid. Mark the carbon that changes during oxidation and count its C–O bond orders and C–H bonds in each structure. Assign +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H bond and zero per C–C bond. Explain why the sequence is oxidation even when no oxygen atom is added in the first net alcohol → aldehyde transformation.






Worked check





The ethanol CH₂OH carbon has one C–O and two C–H bonds, giving −1. In ethanal, the carbonyl carbon has C=O and C–H, giving +1. In ethanoic acid it has C=O and C–O, giving +3. Raising the carbon oxidation state is oxidation. Removing hydrogen can accomplish that without increasing the number of oxygen atoms; the local bond inventory, rather than simply counting O atoms in the entire formula, gives the useful check.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
section: 2. Predict two oxidation products and one boundary
text:
2. Predict two oxidation products and one boundary
Draw the selected oxidation product of propan-2-ol. Why does the comparable simple oxidation pattern not apply to 2-methylpropan-2-ol without breaking the carbon skeleton? If the target is ethanal from ethanol, why must you consider the possibility of ethanoic acid formation when selecting conditions?






Worked check





Propan-2-ol gives propanone. Its OH-bearing carbon has a C–H bond available for the net carbonyl-forming change. The tertiary alcohol has three C–C bonds at that carbon and no C–H; forming C=O while keeping all three carbon groups would overbond carbon. This does not mean a tertiary alcohol is immune to every oxidant, because harsh conditions can cleave C–C bonds. Ethanal can undergo further oxidation, so an aldehyde target requires appropriate controlled conditions rather than an unspecified oxidation arrow.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
text:
3. Draw reduction in two stages
Use propanone and a hydride equivalent delivered from a reagent such as NaBH₄. Draw addition to carbonyl carbon with the π pair moving to oxygen. Give the alkoxide formula and charge. Then show an explicit proton transfer from water. Name the resulting alcohol. Explain the limit of using H:⁻ in this drawing.






Worked check





The H-delivering pair forms a C–H bond and the C=O pair returns to O. The resulting (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ is an alkoxide. Its oxygen lone pair takes H from water while the water O–H pair returns to water oxygen, giving propan-2-ol and OH⁻. H:⁻ is shorthand for hydride-equivalent delivery from the reagent, not free hydride coexisting in water. Detailed boron-containing intermediates are outside this simplified introductory scheme.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
text:
4. What would count as evidence?
Inspect the simulated IR comparison. Identify the changes consistent with converting an alcohol to a carbonyl compound. What other observations would you request before identifying a pure isolated product? Could a 95% isolated yield alone establish identity or purity?






Worked check





Loss of a broad alcohol O–H absorption and appearance of a carbonyl band support the proposed functional-group change. A full spectrum, NMR or other appropriate identification evidence and a check of sample purity would be useful. Isolated mass can include solvent or impurities, so a large yield does not alone identify the compound or establish purity. The supplied traces are schematic teaching data, not observations from an actual oxidation.

title: Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table
section: 5. R task: prepare a reaction amount table
text:
5. R task: prepare a reaction amount table
The balanced teaching equation is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid, with all coefficients one. The shared CSV supplies reagent masses and molar masses. This is a calculation context, not a synthesis protocol. Keep the raw data unchanged.
The amount in mol is mass in g divided by molar mass in g/mol. Divide each reactant amount by its stoichiometric coefficient. The smallest available reaction extent limits the maximum product amount. Here aspirin’s coefficient is one and its supplied molar mass is 180.16 g/mol.
Predict which of 10.0 and 15.0 mmol will limit a 1:1 reaction, then add this code to your report:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_product_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
theoretical_product_mass_g
Knit the report. Give the limiting reagent, theoretical product amount in mmol and mass in g. Change a copy of the acetic anhydride input to 0.51045 g and predict the new limiting reagent before recalculating. Do not overwrite the original CSV to make this alternative scenario.






Numerical and chemical check





The supplied amounts are 0.0100 mol acid and 0.0150 mol anhydride. Salicylic acid limits the product to 10.0 mmol, corresponding to 1.8016 g aspirin. With 0.51045 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, anhydride is 5.00 mmol and limits product to 5.00 mmol, or 0.9008 g. Comparing masses alone would be wrong because the reagents have different molar masses. In a different balanced reaction, coefficients other than one must also be included.

text:
Leave with
A redox transformation map, a two-stage reduction mechanism and a knitted amount table. Continue with the practical report guide to distinguish theoretical yield, isolated yield, conversion and purity.

title: Elimination and addition
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Track bond changes in an E2 step.
Use anti-periplanar geometry in a simple example.
Explain representative ionic alkene additions.


Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
What leaves during elimination?

A formal elimination of HBr from bromoethane forms ethene; a base receives H and bromide leaves.A β-hydrogen and leaving group are lost from neighbouring carbons as a C=C bond forms.

The primary bromoethane equation is a bookkeeping illustration, not a claim of dominant E2 under aqueous hydroxide. Primary substrates often give substitution.

title: Elimination and addition
section: E2 moves three pairs in one step
text:
E2 moves three pairs in one step

The base-to-H, C–H-to-C–C and C–Br-to-Br arrows form the E2 electron-flow cycle.Draw the base lone pair → β-H; C–H pair → C–C π bond; C–Br pair → Br.

The three arrows describe one elementary step. Identify alpha as the carbon carrying the leaving group and beta as its neighbour. Unshown substituents do not mean incomplete valence.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Reactive geometry is three-dimensional

A Newman projection shows a front-carbon hydrogen opposite a back-carbon bromine at 180 degrees.An anti-periplanar C–H/C–Br arrangement supports the common E2 pathway. Read the viewing direction before choosing H.

The front carbon is the dot and the rear carbon the circle. Check that students can rebuild the Newman view using a physical model before drawing a product.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Rotation can expose a reactive hydrogen
text:
Rotation can expose a reactive hydrogen

Partial Newman projections compare anti and eclipsed H/Br arrangements.Rotation about a single bond changes conformation, not connectivity. In a flexible molecule it can create an anti arrangement.

Other groups are omitted intentionally. Constrained rings can restrict the needed geometry; the diagram is not a general statement that every beta-H is equally available.

title: Elimination and addition
section: More than one beta carbon can react
text:
More than one beta carbon can react

2-bromobutane can lose beta hydrogen in two positions to give but-1-ene or but-2-ene, with E/Z forms for the latter.Locate possible β-carbons first. Geometry and conditions determine which of the possible alkenes are favoured.

The more substituted alkene is often favoured with a small base, but bulky bases and geometry can change the distribution. Avoid presenting a universal product ratio.

title: Elimination and addition
section: An alkene supplies a pi pair to H
text:
An alkene supplies a pi pair to H

Propene protonation by HBr forms the secondary carbocation and bromide in the representative ionic route.The C=C π bond is an electron-pair source. Protonation giving the more stable carbocation explains this regioselectivity.

For propene, H attaches to the terminal carbon in the shown pathway. This is the ionic case without peroxides; radical HBr addition is outside the required toolkit.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
The carbocation is then captured

A bromide lone pair attacks the secondary propyl carbocation to produce 2-bromopropane.The observed connectivity follows two steps: protonation, then nucleophile capture.

The intermediate has three carbon bond directions and a positive charge. If a new stereocentre forms in another example, both accessible faces must be considered.

title: Elimination and addition
section: Some additions avoid a free carbocation
text:
Some additions avoid a free carbocation

A bridged bromonium intermediate is opened by bromide attack from the opposite side.Br₂ addition commonly proceeds through a bromonium bridge and anti opening, rather than the free-carbocation HBr model.

This diagram shows the ring-opening stage only. The curved arrow returning the C–Br bridge pair to Br relieves the positive charge as the new C–Br bond forms.

title: Elimination and addition
section: E1 and SN1 can share an intermediate
text:
E1 and SN1 can share an intermediate

A tertiary carbocation can be captured by water or lose a beta hydrogen to form an alkene.Ionisation followed by β-H loss gives E1; ionisation followed by capture gives SN1.

In E1, a weak base such as water can remove the beta proton after ionisation. Product proportions depend on conditions; heat can favour elimination in many cases.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Read the local bond inventory

A C–C single bond becomes C=C in elimination; addition consumes a pi bond and makes new sigma bonds.Check the specific atoms that gain and lose bonds. These labels do not make every pair of reactions exact reverses under identical conditions.

Ask students to supply omitted reagents and products for a real example. A bare C–C/C=C cartoon is only a summary of local changes.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Choose the attacked atom
Attack at a saturated carbon can give substitution. Removal of β-H can give elimination. Donation of an alkene π pair to H gives addition.
The same electron-flow language applies to all three.

title: Elimination and addition
section: A product name is not a mechanism
text:
A product name is not a mechanism
For HBr + propene, draw the two electron-flow steps and identify the intermediate.
Then explain why the simple carbocation model is inappropriate for Br₂ addition via bromonium.

title: Elimination and addition
text:
Check a possible product
Can methyl bromide undergo ordinary β-elimination? Draw its carbon skeleton before answering.
For 2-bromobutane, name each constitutional alkene and state which can have E/Z forms.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
1. Which carbon is secondary?
Classify the carbon bearing Br in CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃.






Check your answer





It is secondary because it is directly bonded to two carbon atoms. The molecule containing four carbons does not make the reacting centre tertiary.

title: Self-check: Substitution
text:
2. What does SN2 leave behind?
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br, give products and net charge.






Check your answer





CH₃OH + Br⁻; total charge is minus one. The C–Br pair goes to Br while hydroxide makes C–O.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 3. What happens when both concentrations double?
text:
3. What happens when both concentrations double?
Use the supplied simple SN2 rate law k[RX][Nu]. Keep temperature and solvent fixed.






Check your answer





The initial rate becomes fourfold because each concentration contributes a factor of two. This does not by itself predict a fourfold isolated yield.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
text:
4. Does inversion always mean R becomes S?
Explain why priorities must still be checked after an SN2 replacement.






Check your answer





The reacting geometry inverts, but replacing one substituent can change CIP priorities. Assign the new priorities before translating geometry into an R/S label.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 5. What follows water capture in SN1?
text:
5. What follows water capture in SN1?
Water adds to a carbocation. Is the immediate product an ordinary neutral alcohol?






Check your answer





No. Oxygen has three bonds and formal charge plus one, giving a protonated alcohol. A base such as another water must remove a proton to give the neutral alcohol.

title: Self-check: Substitution
section: 6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
text:
6. Is every SN1 product exactly racemic?
A carbocation is planar. What does that suggest, and what qualification is needed?






Check your answer





Both faces can be accessible, giving both configurations when a stereocentre forms. Ion pairs and the molecular environment can bias attack, so exact 50:50 is not universal.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
text: Allow 75–90 minutes. Draw bonds, lone pairs and charges explicitly at the reacting centre. Your explanation should connect structure, geometry and conditions. A product formula alone is not a mechanism.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
text:
1. Classify the correct carbon
Draw CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃CBr. Circle the carbon attached to bromine and count how many carbon atoms are directly attached to it. Which are methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary? Which has no neighbouring carbon bearing a potential β-hydrogen?






Hint





The classification concerns the carbon attached to Br. A long chain can still have a primary reaction centre if Br is at an end.









Worked check





CH₃Br is methyl (zero carbon neighbours); CH₃CH₂Br is primary (one); CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ is secondary (two); (CH₃)₃CBr is tertiary (three). Methyl bromide has no β-carbon. This matters for both steric approach in substitution and the possibility of β-elimination. Carbon count alone does not settle the outcome; the nucleophile/base, leaving group, solvent and temperature matter.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
text:
2. Draw the methyl SN2 example
Use OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻. Show the hydroxide lone pair, the leaving-group bond pair and the products. Draw the approach opposite Br. Is there a carbocation intermediate? If the simple rate law is rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻], what happens to the initial rate when both initial concentrations double at fixed temperature and solvent?






Worked check





The donor pair forms C–O as the C–Br pair returns to Br. The changes are concerted, with no carbocation intermediate. Net charge is −1 throughout. Doubling both concentrations gives four times the initial rate in the supplied model, because (2[CH₃Br]) × (2[OH⁻]) = 4[CH₃Br][OH⁻]. This is a kinetic prediction, not an equilibrium or isolated-yield prediction.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
section: 3. Inversion versus a change in the letter
text:
3. Inversion versus a change in the letter
Build a tetrahedral carbon model with four different groups: Br, H, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. Place it so you can look along the C–Br bond. Replace Br by OH through backside attack while preserving the identities of the three retained groups. Draw before and after using wedge/dash bonds. Assign priorities independently to each drawing and then give the R/S labels.






Worked check





The tetrahedral arrangement inverts at the reacting carbon. For this particular 2-bromobutane → butan-2-ol comparison, Br and OH are each highest priority in their respective structures; ethyl ranks above methyl and H is lowest. Thus an S starting configuration gives R in the product, or vice versa. The general mechanistic rule is geometric inversion. In other replacements, priorities may change, so do not infer a new letter without checking them.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
section: 4. Work through an SN1 model in water
text:
4. Work through an SN1 model in water
For a tertiary alkyl bromide (CH₃)₃CBr, draw these separate stages: ionisation; attack by water; removal of a proton by another water molecule. Show charges after every stage. Explain why the first stage is more plausible for this substrate than for CH₃Br. Name one possible product of a competing pathway starting from the same carbocation.






Hint





Water oxygen starts with two bonds. After it bonds to carbon but before it loses a proton, count its bonds again.









Worked check





The C–Br pair moves to Br, giving (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻. A water lone pair attacks the carbocation, giving (CH₃)₃COH₂⁺. Another water removes H⁺ to give (CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺. Bromide remains a spectator after ionisation. The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by its carbon substituents relative to a methyl carbocation. Loss of β-H from the carbocation can instead yield 2-methylpropene through E1. Neither the substrate name nor water alone tells you the precise product ratio.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
section: 5. Why is a neutral alcohol not automatically a good substrate?
text:
5. Why is a neutral alcohol not automatically a good substrate?
A proposed step shows OH⁻ leaving directly from an ordinary neutral alcohol to form a carbocation. Identify the problem. Draw an acid–base activation step that could make water the departing group, and explain why the resulting substitution/elimination outcome still requires substrate and conditions.






Worked check





Hydroxide is a poor leaving group in the selected conditions. Protonating the alcohol oxygen gives an oxonium species that can lose neutral water. This activation does not make every alcohol react by SN1: carbocation stability, availability of nucleophiles/bases and other conditions determine whether a concerted, stepwise or competing elimination route is plausible.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
text:
6. Explain a substrate-and-condition choice
Compare methyl bromide with a strong nucleophile to a tertiary bromide in a polar aqueous medium. Write a short justified pathway proposal for each. Include one limitation of your proposal; for example, a competing process or information needed before predicting an experimental product proportion.

title: Practice: explain a substitution pathway
text:
Leave with
Two complete mechanisms, an inversion drawing and an explanation linking each pathway to its reacting centre and medium. Consult the reading guide for selected Solomons chapter 6 support.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Identify an electron-pair source and acceptor.
Draw valid arrows for an elementary step.
Distinguish intermediates, transition states and catalysts.


Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Arrows follow electron pairs

A lone pair forms the new O–H bond while the original O–H bonding pair returns to oxygen.Every full-headed curved arrow starts at a lone pair or bond. Two arrows are needed for this proton transfer.

Point to each arrow tail and ask what pair was there before the step. Do not accept an arrow starting at a positive charge or at a bare hydrogen.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Both bonding electrons can stay together
text:
Both bonding electrons can stay together

The C–Br bonding pair moves to bromine, giving formally separated positive and negative ions.Heterolysis gives the two bonding electrons to one atom. Charge separation must appear in the products.

This is bookkeeping, not a prediction that a methyl carbocation forms readily. Methyl substrates instead favour concerted substitution in the examples used here.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Name the donor and acceptor

A hydroxide lone pair is the source and the polar carbonyl carbon is an electron-pair acceptor.A nucleophile donates a pair to form a bond; an electrophile accepts it. A neutral molecule may be either.

This picture locates the source and acceptor. It is not a complete mechanism: the carbonyl pi pair must move too when the new bond forms.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Do not give carbon five bonds
text:
Do not give carbon five bonds

Hydroxide addition moves the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen and makes a tetrahedral alkoxide.New C–O bond formation and C=O π-bond cleavage occur in the same elementary addition step.

Count the central carbon bond orders before and after. The product oxygen with one bond has three lone pairs and formal charge minus one.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: One elementary step can use several arrows
text:
One elementary step can use several arrows

Two electron pairs move together in methyl bromide substitution by hydroxide.Concerted means one step with no intermediate between bond breaking and bond making.

The total charge remains minus one. There is no methyl carbocation minimum hidden in this concerted example.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: A proton must come from a species
text:
A proton must come from a species

Ethoxide receives a proton from water, and hydroxide is produced.Write the proton donor and its conjugate base. A work-up is a chemical step, not a source of unexplained H atoms.

Use this to prepare for carbonyl reduction. Students often draw the alkoxide directly as an alcohol and lose both the proton donor and charge.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Transition states are energy maxima

A one-step free-energy profile has one maximum between reactants and products.The transition state is not an isolable intermediate. Its barrier helps determine the reaction rate.

The curve is schematic. The vertical axis is free energy, not concentration, and the horizontal axis is reaction progress, not elapsed time.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
An intermediate occupies a minimum

A two-step schematic path has two transition states and an intermediate free-energy minimum.Count steps by maxima, not by the number of curved arrows. An intermediate has a finite lifetime.

A minimum may be short-lived and difficult to observe. The diagram does not by itself specify whether it can be bottled.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Catalysis changes the pathway

Catalysed and uncatalysed paths have the same reactant and product energies but different barriers.A catalyst can increase the rate while leaving the overall equilibrium constant unchanged.

The drawn catalysed profile is simplified. Real catalysis often adds multiple elementary steps; the catalyst is regenerated overall.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Use an atom and charge audit
text:
Use an atom and charge audit

Substitution conserves C, H, O and Br and has total charge minus one on both sides.After every step, check valence, atoms and net charge. Add implied hydrogens when the audit is unclear.

An electron-flow arrow does not add atoms. A missing counterion may be a spectator, but the reacting species must still have correct individual charges.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: Nucleophilicity and basicity ask different questions
text:
Nucleophilicity and basicity ask different questions
A base accepts a proton; a nucleophile attacks an electrophilic centre. The same species can do both, but the preferred outcome depends on the substrate and conditions.
Identify the atom attacked before naming the process.

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Repair an impossible step
A student draws OH⁻ adding to a carbonyl but leaves the C=O double bond intact.
Draw all bonds to that carbon. Which electron pair must move, and where does the negative charge end up?

title: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
Explain an energy diagram
Sketch a two-step path. Mark both transition states and the intermediate.
Which feature would change if a catalyst offers a faster path? Which endpoint energy difference stays the same?
