title: Self-check: stereochemistry
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?
text:
1. Is carbon attached to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃ a stereocentre?






Check your answer





No: the two methyl substituents are identical. A simple tetrahedral stereocentre requires four different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.
text:
2. Give lactic-acid CIP priorities for OH, COOH, CH₃ and H.






Check your answer





OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. Oxygen outranks carbon. For the carbon tie, the COOH carbon has O,O,O in the comparison, whereas CH₃ has H,H,H.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.
text:
3. Assign the lactic-acid Fischer with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right.






Check your answer





S. The 1→2→3 trace appears clockwise, but the lowest-priority H is horizontal and points toward the viewer, so invert.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 4. Can propene have E and Z forms?
text:
4. Can propene have E and Z forms?






Check your answer





No. Its terminal alkene carbon bears two identical H substituents. Each alkene carbon needs two different substituents.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?
text:
5. Must a molecule with two stereocentres be chiral?






Check your answer





No. A meso compound has stereocentres but is achiral because of its overall symmetry. Meso-tartaric acid is an example.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?
text:
6. What is the ee of 70% R and 30% S?






Check your answer





40% ee in favour of R. The major enantiomer makes up 70%, not 40%, of the two-enantiomer mixture.

title: Self-check: stereochemistry
section: 7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?
text:
7. Does S establish negative optical rotation?






Check your answer





No. R/S specifies configuration and (+)/(−) is a measured rotation sign; there is no universal mapping.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
text: Allow 90 minutes for drawing/model problems and 25 minutes for the R task. Use models or redraw structures in a standard orientation before assigning a relationship. Identify connectivity before deciding about chirality.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
section: 1. Is the difference connectivity or spatial arrangement?
text:
1. Is the difference connectivity or spatial arrangement?
Classify each pair, giving a structural reason:

Ethanol and dimethyl ether.
Anti and gauche conformations of butane.
The two mirror-related lactic-acid drawings below.
E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene.




Mirror-related Fischer drawings of lactic acid.








Worked check





Pair 1 contains constitutional isomers because oxygen has different neighbours. Pair 2 contains conformers related by single-bond rotation. Pair 3 contains enantiomers: same connectivity, mirror-related and nonsuperimposable, with opposite configuration at the single stereocentre. Pair 4 contains configurational stereoisomers that are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers. Ordinary rotation around the intact double bond does not interconvert them freely.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
section: 2. Find stereocentres without relying on wedges
text:
2. Find stereocentres without relying on wedges
Compare CH₃CH(OH)COOH with CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Draw every substituent at the carbon bearing OH. Which molecule has a tetrahedral stereocentre there? Does adding a wedge to the second drawing change your answer?






Hint





List the complete substituent groups, not just the directly attached atom. For this first test, ask whether any two groups are identical.









Worked check





Lactic acid has H, OH, CH₃ and COOH at its tetrahedral carbon: four different groups, so it is a stereocentre. Propan-2-ol has H, OH, CH₃ and CH₃: two groups are identical, so it is not a stereocentre. A wedge changes how a bond is represented, not the connectivity or identity of the substituents.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
section: 3. Assign R/S with an explicit viewing convention
text:
3. Assign R/S with an explicit viewing convention
Use the lactic-acid Fischer projection with COOH top, CH₃ bottom, OH left and H right. State the projection’s depth convention. Rank the substituents, showing how you resolve the tie between the two carbon groups. Trace 1→2→3 and explain any reversal needed before giving the descriptor. Assign the mirror image as a separate check.






Worked check





Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer; vertical bonds point away. OH is priority 1 because O outranks C and H. COOH outranks CH₃: for the carbon tie, the duplicate-atom convention compares O,O,O with H,H,H. H is priority 4. The apparent 1(left)→2(top)→3(bottom) path is clockwise. Because 4 points toward the viewer, reverse the simple clockwise assignment: this drawing is S. Its mirror has R configuration. Neither descriptor specifies the sign of measured optical rotation.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
section: 4. Assign E/Z, or explain why it does not apply
text:
4. Assign E/Z, or explain why it does not apply
Draw but-2-ene twice, with methyl groups first on the same side and then on opposite sides of the double bond. Rank substituents separately at each alkene carbon and assign E/Z. Then test CH₂=CHCH₃ and (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. Which can have an E/Z descriptor at the indicated double bond?






Worked check





For but-2-ene, CH₃ outranks H at both carbons. Methyls on the same side give Z and on opposite sides E. Propene has two H atoms at the terminal carbon, so E/Z does not apply. In (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, one alkene carbon bears two identical methyl groups, so E/Z also does not apply. Looking for two different groups at each end is a prerequisite, not an optional naming detail.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
text:
5. Test an overall symmetry claim
Draw tartaric acid as a Fischer projection with COOH top and bottom and OH on the right at both central carbons (H on the left). Identify its two stereocentres and the relationship between its upper and lower halves. Explain why “it has two stereocentres, therefore it must be chiral” fails. What would you need to check before calling another R,S compound meso?






Worked check





This is meso-tartaric acid, with opposite configurations at the two centres and an internal symmetry relationship between equivalent halves. It is achiral despite stereocentres. The descriptors alone do not establish meso: the whole molecule and the equivalence of its substituents must permit the appropriate symmetry/superimposability. A generic molecule labelled R,S need not have the same molecular symmetry as tartaric acid.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
section: 6. R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
text:
6. R task: distinguish percentage from enantiomeric excess
Question: how unbalanced is each supplied two-enantiomer mixture? The simulated table data/enantiomers.csv contains sample identifiers and percentages of R and S. This model assumes R and S are the only components being counted and have no missing composition. First check that R% + S% = 100.
For this model, ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent). Report the major enantiomer too. Predict the ee for E1 (70% R, 30% S) before running the code.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
mixtures <- read_csv("data/enantiomers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(total_percent = R_percent + S_percent,
         ee_percent = abs(R_percent - S_percent),
         excess = case_when(R_percent > S_percent ~ "R",
                            S_percent > R_percent ~ "S",
                            TRUE ~ "racemic"))
knitr::kable(mixtures, digits = 1)
ggplot(mixtures, aes(sample_id, ee_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Enantiomeric excess (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
Write one sentence about each sample, specifying both composition and ee. If a sample has 80% ee in favour of R, calculate R% and S% by solving R + S = 100 and R − S = 80. Explain why the graph alone does not establish sample purity or optical-rotation sign.






Numerical and chemical check





E1 has 40% ee in favour of R; E2 (50:50) is racemic, 0% ee; E3 (95:5) has 90% ee in favour of R. An 80% R ee corresponds to 90% R and 10% S. Enantiomeric composition does not establish the absence of other chemical contaminants. Without a validated composition measurement and suitable assumptions this is only a calculation on supplied data. R/S alone does not give optical-rotation sign or a biological effect.

title: Classify stereoisomers and explain an enantiomeric excess
text:
Leave with
A classification of spatial relationships, one fully justified R/S assignment, valid E/Z tests and a reproducible ee table. Complete the self-check. Optional reference: selected Solomons chapter 5 sections, using the reading guide.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Draw a Newman projection along a stated bond.
Distinguish staggered/eclipsed and anti/gauche arrangements.
Explain a chair flip and inspect a supplied two-state population model.


Begin with a model or two pen caps connected by a bond. Ask which atoms remain neighbours after turning one end. The R task is a guided numerical comparison, not a thermodynamics derivation.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
section: Rotate a bond; keep the neighbours
text:
Rotate a bond; keep the neighbours

Rotation about the ethane carbon-carbon sigma bond preserves connectivity.Conformation changes can occur through bond rotation. Configuration changes require a different operation, often bond breaking.

Do not claim every single bond rotates freely. Rings, steric interactions and partial double-bond character can restrict rotation.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
State the viewing direction

Looking along a CC bond gives a front dot and rear circle in a Newman projection.The front carbon is the one nearest your eye. Identify it before placing the substituents.

Have students physically point along a model bond. Copying the page silhouette without specifying a view is a common source of error.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Compare the angular offset

Ethane Newman projections compare staggered and eclipsed bond alignments.Staggered has a 60° offset between front and rear bonds. Eclipsed bonds align in the projection.

Coincident bonds in an eclipsed projection do not represent a shared extra bond. Distinguish overlapping views from connectivity.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Rotation crosses an energy barrier

A qualitative ethane torsional profile has eclipsed maxima and staggered minima.The conformers interconvert; lower energy does not mean a structure is permanently trapped.

This curve is a qualitative energy model. Do not use its arbitrary vertical scale to infer a numerical population or rate.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Butane introduces distinct staggered arrangements

Newman projections place the butane methyl groups 180 or 60 degrees apart.Anti and gauche describe the methyl-group dihedral angle here. Both arrangements are staggered.

The terms do not replace front/back or R/S. Count the C1-C2-C3-C4 dihedral, not an arbitrary pair of H atoms.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Compare minima, not just shapes

Qualitative butane profile places anti below gauche and methyl-methyl eclipsing highest.For butane, anti is lower than gauche. The profile also contains less favourable eclipsed arrangements.

Keep qualitative electronic/steric reasoning at the intended level. A simplified energy profile is not a measured free-energy dataset.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
section: A ring constrains the available motion
text:
A ring constrains the available motion

Planar skeletal drawings of cyclopropane and cyclohexane show different ring connectivity.A flat polygon is a connectivity drawing. Cyclohexane is not normally a planar regular hexagon.

Cyclopropane has substantial angle strain. Do not imply cyclohexane has no energetic differences among conformations.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Read axial and equatorial locally

A cyclohexane chair with one axial and one equatorial direction at a selected carbon.Each carbon has an axial and an equatorial position. Axial positions alternate up and down around the ring.

Students should not identify axial as up: there are axial-down positions too. Equatorial does not mean lying in the page.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
A chair flip preserves up/down

A schematic chair flip exchanges an up methyl substituent between axial and equatorial sites.Axial becomes equatorial and vice versa; an up substituent stays up. A ring flip does not invert the configuration.

This diagram highlights local bond directions. Use a molecular model to complete the whole chair flip and preserve all six connected atoms.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Inspect a supplied free-energy model

A two-conformer free-energy model gives unequal populations at 298.15 kelvin.Use relative free energies and a temperature to calculate weights. The lower-free-energy conformer is more populated.

The supplied ΔG values already account for degeneracy. Do not import qualitative torsional energies from another figure as these numerical free energies.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
The two-state calculation
For supplied relative free energies, w_i=\exp[-\Delta G_i/(RT)] and p_i=w_i/\sum_j w_j.
Use consistent J/mol and J/(mol K) units; temperature is kelvin.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
R continues a familiar workflow
conformers <- readr::read_csv("data/conformers.csv")
conformers$weight <- exp(-conformers$delta_G_J_mol /
                           (8.314462618 * 298.15))
conformers$fraction <- conformers$weight / sum(conformers$weight)
Check that fractions sum to one.

title: Conformations and molecular flexibility
text:
Explain a model boundary
An equilibrium population alone does not give the rate of interconversion.
Rates depend on activation barriers; populations depend on the free-energy difference between states.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Repair your drawing or explanation after checking it. These are formative questions, not a formal examination.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
section: 1. Where does the first arrow start?
text:
1. Where does the first arrow start?
In hydroxide deprotonation of an alcohol, should an electron-flow arrow begin at hydroxide oxygen’s lone pair, at the acidic hydrogen, or at the product?






Check your answer





At the hydroxide lone pair. The arrow ends at the acidic H. A second arrow moves the original O–H bonding pair onto the alcohol oxygen.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
text:
2. Which charge follows proton loss?
CH₃NH₃⁺ loses H⁺. Give the formula and charge of its conjugate base.






Check your answer





CH₃NH₂, neutral. Losing a positive proton reduces the net charge by one.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
section: 3. Does the ion switch between resonance forms?
text:
3. Does the ion switch between resonance forms?
Explain the relationship between the two equivalent ethanoate contributors.






Check your answer





They are representations of one delocalised ion, not two equilibrating ions. Electron placement differs; nuclear positions and connectivity do not.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
section: 4. At pH one unit below pKa, what is ionised?
text:
4. At pH one unit below pKa, what is ionised?
Choose 9.1%, 10%, 50% or 90.9%, and show your ratio-to-fraction conversion.






Check your answer





The ratio A⁻/HA is 0.1, so the fraction is 0.1/1.1, about 9.1%.

title: Self-check: acids, bases and ionisation
section: 5. Can an ionisation curve predict the isolated mass after extraction?
text:
5. Can an ionisation curve predict the isolated mass after extraction?
State at least two additional quantities you would need.






Check your answer





No. Partition information and phase volumes are needed, with initial amount and any losses relevant to a mass prediction. Aqueous ionisation is only one part of the model.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
text: Allow about 60 minutes for paper problems and 40 minutes for the R task. You need lone pairs, formal charges, ggplot2, and a working R Markdown report. Use the restart guide if needed.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
text:
1. Follow the electron pair
Draw ethanoic acid and hydroxide with the relevant lone pairs. Draw two curved arrows to produce ethanoate and water. Label both conjugate pairs and check the total charge on each side. Then reverse the drawing: which species would have to act as the acid and base in the reverse reaction?






Hint





Begin one arrow on a hydroxide lone pair and end it at the acidic hydrogen. The other arrow starts at the acid’s O–H bond.









Worked check





The acid is CH₃COOH and the base is OH⁻. Products are CH₃COO⁻ and H₂O. The conjugate pairs are acid/ethanoate and water/hydroxide. Total charge is −1 on both sides. In the reverse direction water would donate H⁺ to ethanoate. This reverse event is possible, but equilibrium strongly favours the forward direction under the compatible aqueous pKa approximation.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
text:
2. Explain acidity using structure
Draw ethoxide and both equivalent ethanoate resonance contributors. Which conjugate base delocalises its negative charge over equivalent oxygen atoms? Explain why moving a hydrogen atom would no longer be resonance. Use supplied approximate aqueous pKa values: ethanol 16 and ethanoic acid 4.8.






Worked check





Ethanoate delocalises the charge over its two oxygens; its two C–O bonds are equivalent in the actual ion. The contributors have the same nuclei in the same positions and differ in electron placement. A hydrogen shift changes connectivity and describes a chemical transformation. Ethanoic acid is the stronger acid; pKa compares equilibria, while conjugate-base stabilisation provides the structural explanation.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
text:
3. Predict a proton transfer
For CH₃COOH + CH₃NH₂ ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + CH₃NH₃⁺ use pKa 4.8 for the reactant acid and 10.6 for methylammonium. Predict the favoured side and estimate the equilibrium constant as 10^(product_acid_pKa - reactant_acid_pKa).






Worked check





The products contain the weaker acid, with larger pKa. The estimated constant is 10^5.8, about 630,957. This estimate requires compatible solvent and standard-state conventions. It predicts a strongly product-favoured equilibrium, not an irreversible reaction or an experimental reaction rate.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
section: 4. R task: how much of the acid is ionised?
text:
4. R task: how much of the acid is ionised?
Question: for a monoprotic acid with supplied pKa 4.8, how does its aqueous ionised fraction change between pH 1 and 9? This is a calculated teaching model, not measured acid dissociation data. Use the dilute-solution approximation.
The ratio is \(r=[A^-]/[HA]=10^{pH-pK_a}\), so the fraction is \(r/(1+r)=1/(1+10^{pK_a-pH})\). pH, pKa and the fraction are dimensionless. At pH = pKa predict 0.5. At one pH unit above pKa predict 10/11.
Add the following to your report, below a sentence stating your prediction:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ionisation <- data.frame(pH = seq(1, 9, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(fraction_A_minus = 1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - pH)))
ggplot(ionisation, aes(pH, fraction_A_minus)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#176b91", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "pH", y = "Fraction present as A−") +
  theme_minimal()
1 / (1 + 10^(4.8 - c(3.8, 4.8, 5.8)))
Knit the report. Explain why the curve rises, why its midpoint is 4.8, and why a fraction of 0.909 does not mean each molecule is 90.9% deprotonated. Change pKa to 6.0, predict the shift and then compare the curves. State why the plot alone cannot predict extraction recovery into an organic solvent.






Numerical and chemical check





At pH 3.8, 4.8 and 5.8 the fractions are approximately 0.0909, 0.5 and 0.9091. A larger pKa shifts the midpoint to higher pH; this weaker acid needs higher pH to achieve the same fraction. Fractions describe a population of molecular species. Extraction needs partition coefficients and phase volumes as well as aqueous ionisation. The supplied curve is not a titration curve: pH is the input, not the calculated consequence of adding a specified titrant volume.

title: Acids and bases: from a drawing to an ionisation curve
text:
Leave with
A checked proton-transfer mechanism, a conjugate-base comparison, and a knitted report containing a labelled plot and your own chemical interpretation.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Distinguish a polar bond from a polar molecule.
Identify hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.
Use simple IR evidence alongside structural reasoning.


Revisit functional-group identification before property prediction. Students often say stronger bonds mean a higher boiling point; ask whether the bonds in question are within a molecule or attractions between molecules.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: A bond can share electrons unequally
text:
A bond can share electrons unequally

A carbon-oxygen bond with partial positive carbon and partial negative oxygen.δ+ and δ− mark partial charges. They are not the integer formal charges assigned in a Lewis structure.

Ask which atom more strongly attracts the bonding electrons. Keep bond dipoles distinct from electron-flow arrows used for reactions.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: The molecular shape determines the sum
text:
The molecular shape determines the sum

Opposing CO2 dipoles cancel whereas bent-water dipoles combine.Dipoles are vectors. A molecule with polar bonds can have no net permanent dipole when symmetry makes them cancel.

CO2 is an illustrative comparison, not an organic compound; its simple geometry isolates the vector idea.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Hydrogen bonding has a direction

An alcohol O-H donor contacts a second oxygen lone-pair acceptor.A donor needs a suitable X–H bond, usually O–H or N–H here; an acceptor needs a suitable available lone pair.

The dashed line is an intermolecular contact, not an added covalent bond or proof that a proton has transferred.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: An ether accepts but cannot donate O–H
text:
An ether accepts but cannot donate O–H

Ethanol donates and accepts hydrogen bonds; dimethyl ether accepts but lacks an OH donor.A functional-group name is a shortcut to a bonding pattern. Always check the actual bonds present.

Do not generalise all nitrogen lone pairs as equally available: amides will supply an important later exception.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Boiling separates molecules from each other
text:
Boiling separates molecules from each other

Approximate normal boiling points of dimethyl ether and ethanol contrast similar-sized isomers.Ethanol can form an intermolecular O–H hydrogen-bond network. Its normal boiling point is much higher than that of its ether isomer.

Normal means at about one atmosphere. Boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions; it does not normally break the molecules into atoms.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Water compatibility balances several features

Short and longer hydrocarbon chains attached to an alcohol OH.Within a related alcohol series, increasing the nonpolar region usually lowers water solubility. The OH group alone is not a complete prediction.

Acknowledge temperature and structure effects. Avoid calling all oxygen-containing compounds water soluble.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
IR excites a vibration

An OH bond represented at two separations during stretching.A vibration can absorb IR when it changes the molecular dipole. The spectrum reports vibrational transitions.

Students need the interpretation, not a quantum derivation. An absorbed photon does not imply the bond is broken.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Read axes before assigning a peak
text:
Read axes before assigning a peak

Simulated transmission spectrum with broad OH and sharp carbonyl absorption.This is a simulated trace. In transmission, absorptions point down; wavenumber commonly decreases from left to right.

Different plotting conventions reverse peak direction. Require students to name the y-axis before using down-peak language.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Combine presence and absence of features
text:
Combine presence and absence of features

Alcohol and ketone structures compared with schematic characteristic IR features.Broad alcohol O–H is often around 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; a strong carbonyl is often around 1650–1800 cm⁻¹. Context shifts these ranges.

Absence is evidence only when the spectrum is suitable. Water contamination can introduce OH absorption.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Charge changes hydration

Neutral ethanoic acid and negatively charged ethanoate interacting with water.Ion–dipole interactions can make ionic forms more compatible with water, but actual solubility also depends on other equilibria and the solid or liquid phase.

Prepare the acid–base unit without pretending pH alone determines measured solubility.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
section: Explain a prediction with a controlled comparison
text:
Explain a prediction with a controlled comparison
Compare similar-sized compounds before attributing a boiling-point difference to hydrogen bonding.
A larger molecule may also have stronger dispersion interactions.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Classify the evidence
A spectrum may support a functional group. It rarely gives a unique complete structure by itself.
Ask which competing structures still fit.

title: Properties, interactions and introductory IR
text:
Transfer task
Given an alcohol and a ketone with the same carbon count, sketch an expected IR distinction and explain one difference in their intermolecular interactions.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 1. How many carbons are in a zigzag with four line segments and no branches?
text:
1. How many carbons are in a zigzag with four line segments and no branches?






Check your answer





Five: one at each of the two endpoints and three internal vertices. Saturated acyclic neutral pentane is C₅H₁₂.

title: Self-check: reading organic structures
section: 2. Does C₂H₆O establish that a sample is ethanol?
text:
2. Does C₂H₆O establish that a sample is ethanol?






Check your answer





No. Dimethyl ether shares that molecular formula. Connectivity or suitable experimental evidence is needed.

5. Does a wedge add a fifth bond to carbon?

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
text:
Before you start
A skeletal drawing normally omits carbon symbols and hydrogens bonded to carbon. Unlabelled line endpoints and corners stand for carbon. Heteroatoms such as O and N are labelled. Unless indicated otherwise, use ordinary neutral valences: four bond orders for C, three for N and two for O. Show charges when those patterns change. An explicit charge always needs an electron-count check.



Ethanol in molecular, condensed and skeletal representations.

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
text:
1. Recover the hidden atoms
Draw an unbranched four-segment zigzag with only single bonds. Number every carbon, write CH₃ or CH₂ at each carbon, and obtain the molecular formula. Now change the central C2–C3 bond to a double bond without changing connectivity. Which hydrogen counts change? What is the new formula? This new structure is pent-2-ene; leave E/Z unspecified for now.






Hint





Four segments connect five carbons. A carbon attached to two other carbons by single bonds needs two H atoms. Changing a single bond to a double uses one additional valence at each end of that bond.









Worked check





The saturated chain is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, C₅H₁₂. Introducing C2=C3 gives CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, C₅H₁₀. C2 and C3 each lose one attached H in the formula comparison; no carbon atom is removed. This is a comparison of structures, not a claim that editing a drawing is an experimental synthetic method.

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
text:
2. Tell identity from isomerism
Write Lewis or expanded structural drawings for CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃OCH₃. Count all atoms and list oxygen’s neighbours in each. Explain why turning the first drawing around cannot make it identical to the second. Then redraw ethanol with the OH at the left; is that a third compound?






Worked check





Both molecules have C₂H₆O, but the ethanol oxygen is connected to C and H, while ether oxygen is connected to two C atoms. Changing the view does not change those neighbours, so they are constitutional isomers. Drawing ethanol as HOCH₂CH₃ leaves its connectivity unchanged and does not create a third compound. Both neutral oxygens have two bonds and two lone pairs.

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
text:
3. Read branches and functional groups
For each condensed structure, draw the connected atoms, identify the functional group and label every carbon with its attached H count:

CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
CH₃C(=O)CH₃
CH₃C(=O)OH
CH₃C(=O)OCH₃
CH₃CH₂NH₂

Name the simple structures where you can. Which examples contain a carbonyl? Which have an O–H bond? Which contain an ester rather than an ether alone?






Hint





C(=O) puts a double-bonded oxygen on that carbon. In C(=O)OCH₃, the single-bonded O is connected to the carbonyl carbon and the methyl carbon.









Worked check





The groups are alcohol (propan-1-ol), ketone (propanone), carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid), ester (methyl ethanoate) and amine (ethanamine/ethylamine). Examples 2–4 have a carbonyl; examples 1 and 3 have O–H. Example 4 is the ester: the oxygen lies next to a carbonyl. A carbonyl carbon in these examples has no H except where the drawing explicitly allows one, as in an aldehyde. The carbon totals are 3, 3, 2, 3 and 2 respectively.

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
section: 4. Audit an oxygen and a carbon
text:
4. Audit an oxygen and a carbon
Draw water, hydroxide and hydronium with all oxygen lone pairs. Calculate formal charge using six valence electrons for O. Next, inspect a student’s neutral carbon drawn with one C=O double bond, three C–H single bonds and one C–C single bond. Explain the error and give one valid carbonyl-carbon bonding pattern instead.






Worked check





Water has two O bonds/two lone pairs/charge 0. Hydroxide has one bond/three lone pairs/charge −1. Hydronium has three bonds/one lone pair/charge +1. The proposed carbon has a bond-order sum of six and violates ordinary second-row-carbon valence. In ethanal, CH₃C(=O)H, the carbonyl carbon has one C–C bond, one C–H bond and the C=O double bond, totalling four.

title: Read, redraw and check an organic structure
section: 5. R task: what amount did the balance give us?
text:
5. R task: what amount did the balance give us?
Chemical question: how many moles are represented by a measured mass? Use the supplied relationship amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol. The molar mass has units g/mol; the division leaves mol. Multiply mol by 1000 to obtain mmol. Molar masses are supplied, not memorised.
Download and extract the student project. Open its RStudio project, then open report.Rmd. Keep input CSV files in data/. The table data/amounts.csv is a simulated teaching amount table; it is not a reaction protocol. First work the salicylic-acid row by hand: 1.3812 g at 138.12 g/mol should give 0.01000 mol.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
Predict whether doubling a mass at fixed molar mass doubles the amount. Change an input in a copied R object, not in the raw CSV, and check. Add a sentence explaining what mmol measures. Knit the report from a fresh R session; an unrun object in the console should not be required.






Numerical and chemical check





Salicylic acid gives 10.00 mmol. With the supplied second row, 1.53135 g of acetic anhydride at 102.09 g/mol gives 15.00 mmol. Doubling either mass doubles its amount. These amounts alone do not select the limiting reagent: that requires the balanced reaction’s stoichiometric coefficients, introduced later. The unit mmol counts chemical amount, not volume, concentration or number of independent experiments.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text: This is a complete first teaching draft for a new 7.5-credit Organic Chemistry 1. The sequence below organises five weeks of study; your course’s official timetable and assessment instructions take precedence.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text:
What you should learn

Read molecular representations and identify functional groups and charges.
Explain properties and reactivity using polarity, resonance and acid–base reasoning.
Distinguish conformations and configurations and interpret simple stereochemistry.
Draw valid elementary mechanisms that conserve atoms and charge.
Predict selected substitution, elimination, addition, redox and carbonyl reactions.
Propose a short synthesis and justify conditions and experimental checks.
Use simple IR and one-dimensional NMR evidence to distinguish structures.
Record, calculate and communicate laboratory results in a reproducible report.

These are the teaching outcomes used to organise these materials. The formal course syllabus specifies the approved outcomes and examination rules.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text:
Weekly rhythm








Week
Units
Main work to keep




1
Structures; properties/IR; acids and bases
Annotated structures, a property explanation, proton-transfer mechanism and ionisation plot

The eight R activities occupy about five hours plus time to assemble reports and recover from mistakes; they form a small part of the overall chemistry work.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text:
Check your understanding
Before consulting an answer, record your prediction and reason. If you make a mistake, draw the corrected structure or mechanism and explain what changed. Being able to recognise an answer is a useful start; being able to construct and defend it is the goal.
The self-checks and worked practice are formative. They do not establish examination weightings, compulsory attendance rules or grade boundaries.

title: Learning route and outcomes
text:
What comes next?
This course provides a foundation for biochemistry even if you do not take more organic chemistry. title: Organic Chemistry 1
text:
Organic chemistry connects the shapes of molecules to what they do. In this course you will draw structures, explain reactions, and use experimental evidence to decide whether a chemical explanation holds up.
This five-week teaching route is designed for the new 7.5-credit Organic Chemistry 1 (5KE231) in the Life Science programme. Use your course’s official instructions for dates, laboratory arrangements and assessment requirements.

title: Organic Chemistry 1
text:
Your route through the chemistry


Week 1 · Read and explain
Structures, properties and IR, and acids and bases.
Read the atoms and bonds, explain a physical property, and predict where a proton moves.


Week 2 · Think in three dimensions
Conformations, stereochemistry, and electron flow.
Distinguish a rotated view from a different stereoisomer and draw a defensible mechanism.


Week 3 · Predict a transformation
Substitution, elimination and addition, and alcohols and redox.
Use a small reaction toolkit and explain competing pathways.


Week 4 · Understand carbonyl chemistry
Carbonyl addition, acyl chemistry, and amines and aromatics.
Follow the shared mechanistic patterns that will reappear in biochemistry.


Week 5 · Decide from evidence
Spectroscopy, synthesis and evidence, and integration.
Combine structures, reactions, spectra and calculations into a justified conclusion.

Download the student ZIP, locate it in your file manager and extract it. Open the extracted organic-chemistry.Rproj in RStudio. Work inside the extracted folder rather than opening files inside the ZIP.

library(readr)

amounts

amounts

title: Practical work: prepare, record, evaluate
text:
Keep primary records
Record date, sample identifiers, reagent amounts, relevant conditions, observations and deviations in your laboratory journal as the work happens. Retain instrument files and photographs with their sample labels. An Rmd report draws on those records; it does not replace the original observations.

title: Practical work: prepare, record, evaluate
section: Before a reaction: calculate the amount table
text:
Before a reaction: calculate the amount table
For the teaching equation salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid, all coefficients are one. With 1.3812 g salicylic acid (138.12 g/mol) and 1.53135 g acetic anhydride (102.09 g/mol), the amounts are 10.0 and 15.0 mmol. The acid limits the theoretical aspirin amount to 10.0 mmol. The reaction scheme is a calculation context, not an operating protocol.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
amounts
Compare amount divided by coefficient rather than mass alone. In a different balanced reaction, a coefficient of two would change that comparison.

title: Practical work: prepare, record, evaluate
text:
TLC: retain every spot
For the supplied normal-phase teaching plate, the solvent front travels 5.0 cm from the origin. A starting-material spot travels 1.2 cm and a product spot 3.2 cm. Their Rf values are 0.24 and 0.64. The crude lane contains both spots.
tlc <- read_csv("data/tlc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Rf = spot_distance_cm / front_distance_cm)
tlc
Explain why the crude has two rows. Do not average two different spots into one fictitious compound. Compare Rf only under matched conditions. Co-migration does not prove identity, and a single visible spot does not prove purity.

title: Practical work: prepare, record, evaluate
text:
After isolation: distinguish the claims
With product molar mass 180.16 g/mol, theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. An isolated mass of 1.20 g corresponds to 66.6% isolated yield.
theoretical_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
Yield is not conversion. Loss during work-up can lower isolated yield even after substantial reaction. Residual solvent or impurities can inflate mass. Assess identity and purity using appropriate evidence and uncertainty.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Draw an electron-pair mechanism

Locate the electron source: a lone pair, negative charge or pi bond.
Locate the electron-poor atom or a bond that can accept the pair.
Draw each curved arrow from the electron pair to its destination.
Redraw bonds, lone pairs and charges after the step.
Check atom conservation, charge conservation and valence.

A reaction arrow connects reactants and products. An equilibrium arrow shows opposing reaction directions. A resonance arrow connects contributors of one species. A curved arrow shows electron movement. These symbols have different jobs.

section: Choose among a few reaction patterns

Pattern
What changes

Acid–base

Substrate, nucleophile, leaving group, solvent and mechanism

Quantity
Relationship
Units/check




Chemical amount
\(n=m/M\)
g ÷ (g/mol) = mol

\(n_i/\nu_i\)

Theoretical product amount
\(n_P=\nu_P\min(n_i/\nu_i)\)
mol

\(m_P=n_PM_P\)

\(100m_{isolated}/m_{theoretical}\)

\(ee=|\%R-\%S|\)
Percentage points expressed as % ee; specify major enantiomer



For a mixture containing only two enantiomers, 70% R and 30% S is 40% ee in favour of R. The major-enantiomer percentage is 70%, not 40%.

title: A small chemistry toolkit
text:
Ask what the evidence establishes
IR supports functional-group assignments. NMR reports chemical environments, integrations and coupling patterns. TLC compares behaviour under specified conditions. None is a universal identity or purity certificate on its own. Use several observations and explain the alternatives they rule out.

title: Reading organic structures
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Translate among molecular, condensed and skeletal formulas.
Recover implicit H atoms and audit valence and charge.
Recognise functional groups and calculate a chemical amount from mass.


Start with a drawing students can explain without chemistry vocabulary. Build vocabulary onto concrete bonds and atoms. Expected prior knowledge: atoms, covalent bonds and the mole; supply a brief recap if needed.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
One molecule, several useful views

Molecular, condensed and skeletal representations of ethanol.A formula counts atoms; a structural representation also tells you which atoms are connected.

Ask students which views distinguish ethanol from dimethyl ether. A formula alone cannot.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Read every vertex and endpoint

Pentane chain with five numbered carbon positions and its hydrogen count.An unlabelled vertex or endpoint is carbon. Add enough H atoms to give neutral carbon a bond-order sum of four.

Have students trace the chain with a finger; bends are atoms, not decorative changes of direction.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Count bond orders before adding H
text:
Count bond orders before adding H

Ethane, ethene and ethyne have progressively fewer hydrogen atoms.A double bond contributes two to each connected carbon’s bond-order sum; a triple contributes three.

The drawing is about local valence. Students should not infer that all multiple bonds react in identical ways.

title: Reading organic structures
text:
Same formula, different neighbours

Ethanol and dimethyl ether both have formula C2H6O but different oxygen connectivity.Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity. Redrawing the same connectivity in another orientation does not create one.

Avoid letting students use left/right position on the page as an identity test.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Recognise a functional group as a pattern
text:
Recognise a functional group as a pattern

Alcohol, amine, ether, aldehyde, carboxylic-acid and ester patterns.R and R′ stand for attached organic groups; they are not the element symbols for unknown atoms.

Compare ether and ester carefully: an ester has a carbonyl adjacent to the single-bonded oxygen.

title: Reading organic structures
section: Oxygen can be neutral or charged
text:
Oxygen can be neutral or charged

Water, hydroxide and hydronium compared by bonds, lone pairs and formal charge.Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − half the bonding electrons. For O, start from six valence electrons.

Insist on both lone pairs and charge in student Lewis drawings. Hydroxide oxygen has three lone pairs, not two.

title: Reading organic structures
section: A flat drawing can describe a 3D molecule
text:
A flat drawing can describe a 3D molecule

Tetrahedral, trigonal-planar and linear local carbon geometries.A saturated carbon is approximately tetrahedral; carbonyl/alkene carbon approximately trigonal planar; an alkyne carbon linear.

Wedges indicate direction relative to the page. Their meaning is not that one type of ordinary bond is chemically stronger.

title: Reading organic structures

Practise and carry the skill forward

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
text: Allow 75–90 minutes. This is chemistry practice rather than a new R lesson. Draw each molecule before comparing it. You need the functional groups from structures.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
section: 1. Separate formal charge from partial charge
text:
1. Separate formal charge from partial charge
Draw ethanol with its oxygen lone pairs. Label the C–O bond’s direction of polarisation and the partial charges at its ends. Does a partial negative oxygen have to carry a formal −1 charge? Compare neutral ethanol with ethoxide, CH₃CH₂O⁻, and explain what the superscript minus tells you in the latter case.






Hint





Bond polarity describes unequal electron sharing. Formal charge is calculated from a Lewis electron count and is written as an integer for each contributor.









Worked check





The C–O bond is polarised toward O, giving δ− at oxygen and δ+ at the attached carbon. Neutral ethanol has two bonds and two lone pairs at O, so its oxygen formal charge is zero. Ethoxide has one bond and three lone pairs at O and formal charge −1. Partial charge and formal charge describe different aspects of the electron distribution; they are not interchangeable labels.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
text:
2. Find hydrogen-bond partners
For ethanol, dimethyl ether, propanone and ethanoic acid, mark suitable donor and acceptor sites. Draw one hydrogen-bond contact between ethanol and water, and another between dimethyl ether and water. Which molecule must supply the hydrogen in the second drawing? Avoid adding a covalent bond when drawing the interaction.






Worked check





Ethanol has an O–H donor and an oxygen acceptor. Dimethyl ether and propanone have oxygen acceptors but no O–H/N–H donor. Ethanoic acid has an O–H donor and a carbonyl-oxygen acceptor; the protonated acid hydroxyl oxygen is not normally treated as a useful hydrogen-bond acceptor in this simple inventory. Water can donate H to an ether lone pair. Draw the intermolecular contact as a dashed line O–H···O, keeping covalent connectivity unchanged.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
section: 3. Compare boiling points without changing too many variables
text:
3. Compare boiling points without changing too many variables
Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula, C₂H₆O, and the same molar mass. Their approximate normal boiling temperatures are 78 °C and −24 °C, respectively. Explain why this comparison is useful for discussing hydrogen bonding. What would make comparison of ethanol with a much larger hydrocarbon less controlled? Does the higher boiling point imply a stronger covalent C–O bond?






Worked check





Similar size and formula reduce the size/polarisability difference. Ethanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds between its molecules; pure dimethyl ether lacks an OH donor. A much larger hydrocarbon may have substantial dispersion interactions, so molecular size becomes an important extra variable. Boiling normally separates intact molecules; the comparison concerns intermolecular attractions, not direct evidence about a covalent C–O bond energy.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
text:
4. Explain a solubility trend carefully
Compare ethanol with hexan-1-ol, CH₃(CH₂)₅OH. Identify what stays similar and what changes. Predict which is more compatible with water and justify the prediction using both polar and nonpolar regions. Would your explanation establish the exact solubility in g/L at an unspecified temperature?






Hint





Both contain one OH group. Count how much hydrocarbon is attached to it; do not treat the group as a switch that makes every possible molecule soluble.









Worked check





Ethanol is more water compatible. Both have one OH group, but hexan-1-ol has a larger nonpolar region relative to its hydrogen-bonding head. The comparison supports a qualitative trend, not an exact g/L value. Temperature, detailed molecular structure and interactions in the separated phases also matter.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
text:
5. Read a simulated IR spectrum



A labelled simulated transmission trace showing broad OH and strong carbonyl features.


The illustration is a schematic teaching spectrum, not a measured sample. First name the axes and explain why absorption goes downward. A supplied unknown has a strong absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad alcohol OH feature between about 3200 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Candidates are ethanol, propanone and dimethyl ether. Which candidate best fits this restricted set? What additional evidence would you want before declaring the sample pure propanone?






Worked check





The horizontal axis is wavenumber in cm⁻¹, decreasing to the right; the vertical axis is transmittance. Absorption removes transmitted light, producing a dip. Propanone fits the strong carbonyl and lack of OH; the other candidates lack a carbonyl. The conclusion is relative to the candidate list. It does not establish purity or rule out all other ketones. NMR, further spectral features and suitable purity evidence would strengthen the interpretation.

title: Use structure to explain a property and an IR observation
text:
6. Check a misleading explanation
A student writes: “The IR spectrum has a peak, so the compound is polar and must dissolve in water.” Rewrite the statement as two defensible claims, one about what IR probes and one about what solubility depends on.






Worked check





A suitable IR absorption indicates a vibrational transition involving a change in dipole moment and may support a functional-group assignment. Solubility depends on the balance of solute/solvent and solute/solute interactions, the molecular structure, charge and conditions. A peak alone does not establish water solubility or a nonzero permanent molecular dipole.

text:

Annotated donor/acceptor drawings, a controlled boiling-point explanation and a spectral conclusion that names both supporting evidence and its limits. Complete the self-check before the acid–base unit. Optional reference: selected Solomons chapter 2 topics, as described in the reading guide.

4. Should every oxygen-containing compound dissolve readily in water?

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Identify an acid, base and their conjugates.
Use structure and pKa to predict a proton transfer.

Prerequisites: functional groups, lone pairs, formal charge. Have students draw an oxygen with two bonds/two lone pairs and an oxygen with one bond/three lone pairs. This is the bridge from representations to mechanisms.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: A base uses an electron pair
text:
A base uses an electron pair

Hydroxide accepts an acidic proton; the O–H bond electrons stay on the acid oxygen.Draw both arrows. The proton moves; its original bonding pair stays behind.

Point to the electron pair at the start of each arrow. The arrow is not the path of the proton. Products must conserve total charge: minus one here.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation

Name both conjugate pairs

Ethanoic acid/ethanoate and methylammonium/methylamine each differ by H plus.Removing H⁺ decreases the charge by one. It does not remove an electron pair.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
section: Why is ethanoic acid more acidic than ethanol?
text:
Why is ethanoic acid more acidic than ethanol?

Equivalent resonance contributors distribute negative charge over the two ethanoate oxygens.Compare the conjugate bases. Ethoxide lacks this equivalent delocalisation.

The resonance arrow is not an equilibrium arrow. Both contributors describe one ion; nuclei remain fixed. Ask students to identify which bonds and lone pairs differ and which atoms do not move.

title: Acids, bases and ionisation
text:
pKa is an equilibrium measure

Approximate aqueous pKa values: ethanoic acid 4.8, phenol 10, ethanol 16.pK_a=-\log_{10}K_a. Lower pKa means greater acid dissociation under comparable conditions.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
text: Allow 75–90 minutes for molecular-model and drawing tasks, plus 35 minutes for the optional guided numerical model. Build a physical model if one is available; a carefully labelled drawing can also support the comparison.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
text:
1. Say what your eye sees
Draw CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and number the carbon chain C1 to C4. Look along the C2–C3 bond from C2 toward C3. Draw a Newman projection, naming the front and rear carbons. Each of those carbons bears one CH₃ and two H substituents. Start with the front CH₃ at twelve o’clock and place the rear CH₃ at six o’clock. What is the dihedral angle between the two methyl groups?






Hint





The front carbon is a dot. The rear carbon is the surrounding circle. The three bonds from each carbon are separated by 120° in its own projected set.









Worked check





C2 is the front carbon and C3 the rear. Front CH₃ is C1; rear CH₃ is C4. With front CH₃ at twelve and rear CH₃ at six, the methyl-group dihedral is 180°, the anti arrangement. The other rear bonds lie at two and ten o’clock and the other front bonds at four and eight o’clock, giving a staggered view.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
section: 2. Produce gauche without making a new connectivity
text:
2. Produce gauche without making a new connectivity
Keep the front substituents fixed and turn the rear set by 120°. Draw both possible resulting gauche arrangements and label the methyl–methyl dihedral. Then draw an eclipsed view. Which operations changed connectivity? Which staggered butane arrangement is normally lower in energy, anti or gauche?






Worked check





Starting from anti, rear rotations of ±120° place the rear methyl at two or ten o’clock, giving ±60° methyl–methyl dihedrals relative to the front methyl. They are gauche arrangements. Eclipsed sets have aligned front/rear bonds. None of these rotations changes connectivity. Anti is lower in energy than gauche for butane, although both are populated and interconvert.






Butane Newman projections show the methyl groups anti and gauche.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
text:
3. Read a qualitative energy profile
Use the lecture’s torsional plots to identify minima and maxima. Explain why the ethane minima repeat every 120° and why not all butane minima are equivalent. Can the qualitative vertical scale tell you a numerical Boltzmann population? Does the lowest point show the energy of a transition state?






Worked check





Ethane’s three equivalent H substituents give three equivalent staggered minima in a full turn. In butane, anti and gauche differ in how the larger methyl groups approach each other. The vertical scale is qualitative and cannot supply a numerical free-energy difference for population calculations. A minimum corresponds to a relatively stable conformation, not a transition state. The barrier between minima concerns how the interconversion proceeds.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
section: 4. Follow a substituent through a chair flip
text:
4. Follow a substituent through a chair flip
Draw or build methylcyclohexane with methyl axial and up. Carry out a complete chair flip, following all six ring carbons. Label the methyl group in the second chair using both axial/equatorial and up/down. Repeat for an axial-down substituent. Why would changing axial-up directly to axial-down be the wrong rule for a chair flip?






Hint





Mark each carbon and its up bond before moving the model. The word axial is not a synonym for up; there are axial bonds on both sides of the ring.









Worked check





Axial-up methyl becomes equatorial-up. Axial-down becomes equatorial-down. A ring flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions while preserving the up/down relationship and the configuration. Replacing axial-up by axial-down would reverse the substituent’s side of the ring and is not the same operation. For methylcyclohexane, the equatorial-methyl chair is favoured because it avoids unfavourable 1,3-diaxial interactions, though both chairs remain possible.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
section: 5. R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
text:
5. R task: turn supplied free energies into a population
Question: in a deliberately simplified two-state model, how much of each conformer would be present at equilibrium? The file data/conformers.csv contains relative free energies, ΔG, in J/mol, for A and B: 0 and 3500. These values are supplied teaching values and already include any degeneracy; they are not measured energies for the qualitative butane curve above.
At temperature \(T=298.15\) K and \(R=8.314462618\) J/(mol K), use \(w_i=\exp[-\Delta G_i/(RT)]\) and \(p_i=w_i/\sum_jw_j\). The ratio in the exponent is dimensionless. A is the lower-free-energy state, so predict A will have more than half the population.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conformers <- read_csv("data/conformers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(weight = exp(-delta_G_J_mol / (8.314462618 * 298.15)),
         fraction = weight / sum(weight))
knitr::kable(conformers, digits = 4)
ggplot(conformers, aes(conformer, fraction)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#176b91") +
  labs(x = "Conformer", y = "Predicted equilibrium fraction") +
  theme_minimal()
sum(conformers$fraction)
Add the result to your Rmd report. Check the sum and the direction. As a transfer task, replace 3500 with 0 in a copied data object, predict the answer and recompute. Then set both input energies 1000 J/mol higher, keeping their difference unchanged. What happens to the normalised fractions?






Numerical and model check





At 298.15 K, A has fraction about 0.804 and B about 0.196 (rounding depends on constants). Equal free energies give equal fractions. Adding the same constant to both energies multiplies every weight by the same factor, which cancels on normalisation, leaving fractions unchanged. The calculation assumes the two states adequately describe the system at equilibrium. It does not predict the speed of rotation; an activation free energy would be needed for rates.

title: Turn a model, draw a Newman projection, inspect populations
text:
Leave with
Labelled Newman projections, a chair flip that preserves up/down, and a report figure that separates a numerical model from a qualitative sketch. Finish the self-check. Provisional reference: selected Solomons chapter 4 sections; see the reading guide.

text: Answer before opening each check. Give a reason or a drawing, not only a term.

section: 1. What atom information is unchanged by rotating a C–C single bond?
text:
1. What atom information is unchanged by rotating a C–C single bond?






Check your answer





Connectivity: each atom retains its bonded neighbours. A different conformation is not a constitutional isomer.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 2. What does the circle represent in a Newman projection?
text:
2. What does the circle represent in a Newman projection?






Check your answer





The rear carbon viewed along a specified bond. The front carbon is shown as the central dot.

title: Self-check: conformations
text:
3. Is anti-butane staggered or eclipsed?






Check your answer





Staggered. Its terminal methyl groups have a 180° dihedral angle; gauche-butane is also staggered, with 60° between those groups.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 4. Does a chair flip turn an up substituent down?
text:
4. Does a chair flip turn an up substituent down?






Check your answer





No. Up stays up and down stays down; axial and equatorial exchange. Cis/trans configuration is preserved.

title: Self-check: conformations
section: 5. At equilibrium, what does a positive ΔG for B relative to A predict?
text:
5. At equilibrium, what does a positive ΔG for B relative to A predict?






Check your answer





B has lower statistical weight than A at the same temperature. For the supplied two-state model, use exp(−ΔG/RT) then normalise.

section: 6. Do equilibrium populations determine how quickly a ring flips?
text:
6. Do equilibrium populations determine how quickly a ring flips?






Check your answer





No. Interconversion rates depend on activation barriers, while the equilibrium ratio depends on the free-energy difference of the states.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Classify constitutional isomers, conformers and configurational stereoisomers.
Assign simple R/S and E/Z descriptors with justified priorities.
Explain chirality, meso compounds and enantiomeric excess.


Return to connectivity whenever a 3D problem feels confusing. Introduce Fischer projections explicitly as a convention, not an ordinary flat bond drawing. Use a model to check the worked S assignment.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
First ask what has changed

Constitutional-isomer comparison contrasted with butane conformations.Different connectivity gives constitutional isomers. Same connectivity requires further spatial comparison.

Do not make students assign R/S before they have checked whether both drawings describe the same bonded framework.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Find four different substituents

A tetrahedral lactic-acid carbon attached to COOH, CH3, OH and H.This carbon is a stereocentre because its four substituents differ. Wedge bonds point toward you and hashed bonds away.

A carbon with two identical methyl groups is not a stereocentre even if drawn with a wedge.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Compare mirror images

Mirror-related Fischer projections of lactic acid.Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images. They have the same connectivity and opposite configuration at this single stereocentre.

Physical model manipulation helps distinguish a rotated identical molecule from a nonsuperimposable mirror image.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Rank by atomic number, then the first difference
text:
Rank by atomic number, then the first difference

OH outranks COOH, which outranks CH3, while H is lowest for lactic acid.For the carbon tie: the carboxyl carbon compares as O,O,O while the methyl carbon compares as H,H,H under the duplicate-atom convention.

Do not rank groups by total mass or total atom count. Compare successive shells until the first difference.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
A Fischer projection encodes depth

Horizontal Fischer bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away.You must use the projection convention when assigning configuration. A 90° page rotation is not a safe identity operation for a Fischer drawing.

A 180° in-plane rotation preserves a Fischer configuration. Changing representation requires preserving the actual 3D positions.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Use the direction of group four
text:
Use the direction of group four

Lactic-acid Fischer projection with OH left and H right is assigned S.The apparent 1→2→3 trace is clockwise here, but group 4 points toward you: reverse the assignment to S.

Have students articulate the final inversion. Blindly mapping clockwise to R fails when group four points forward.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: A pi bond restricts the relevant rotation
text:
A pi bond restricts the relevant rotation

Z-but-2-ene has methyl groups on the same side; E has them on opposite sides.Assign priority separately at each alkene carbon. Higher-priority groups together give Z, opposite give E.

E/Z requires two different substituents at each alkene carbon. Propene does not qualify.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: Two stereocentres need not make a chiral molecule
text:
Two stereocentres need not make a chiral molecule

Meso-tartaric-acid Fischer projection has an internal symmetry relationship.A meso compound is achiral despite stereocentres. Examine the complete molecule, not only each carbon in isolation.

The symmetry operation relates identical halves. Do not infer meso simply because a molecule has one R and one S descriptor.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Distinguish composition from excess

Seven R and three S symbols illustrate 70 percent R but 40 percent R enantiomeric excess.For a two-enantiomer mixture, ee=|\%R-\%S|. Also state which enantiomer is in excess.

A 40 percent ee is not 40 percent major enantiomer. The remaining racemic portion contains both forms.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: R/S does not predict the sign of rotation
text:
R/S does not predict the sign of rotation

R/S configuration and measured plus/minus optical rotation are distinct descriptors.Optical rotation is measured under specified conditions. No general rule maps R to (+) or S to (−).

Use this to prevent unsupported claims about biological or sensory effects. Different stereoisomers can behave differently in chiral environments, but the effect must be established.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: What relationships can three structures have?
text:
What relationships can three structures have?
For a compound with multiple stereocentres, stereoisomers may be enantiomers or diastereomers. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.
E/Z pairs are also diastereomeric.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
text:
Calculate and explain enantiomeric excess
mixtures <- readr::read_csv("data/enantiomers.csv")
mixtures$ee_percent <- abs(mixtures$R_percent - mixtures$S_percent)
Check that R% + S% = 100 before treating the sample as a two-enantiomer mixture.

title: Stereochemistry: identity in three dimensions
section: A configuration is not a biological outcome
text:
A configuration is not a biological outcome
A chiral receptor can distinguish enantiomers. That observation does not tell us, without measurements, which enantiomer binds more strongly or what its effect will be.

text:
Practise a spatial explanation
Complete the practice and self-check.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
text: Allow 75–90 minutes. Draw on paper or use a structure editor; chemical drawing is the main work in this unit. Bring the acid–base reasoning and reference toolkit into each explanation.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
text:
First: read the proposed step
A mechanism is a sequence of chemically plausible elementary steps. A complete step specifies the reacting species, electron-pair movements and products. Full-headed curved arrows represent two electrons. Their tails start on a bond or lone pair; their heads identify a new bond or the atom receiving a pair. The arrows do not show a proton’s flight or the direction in which a whole molecule moves. Lone pairs need not all be drawn in every shorthand structure, but draw the reacting pairs while learning.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
section: 1. Proton transfer with an explicit donor
text:
1. Proton transfer with an explicit donor
Draw CH₃OH + OH⁻ ⇌ CH₃O⁻ + H₂O. Add the lone pairs needed for the forward proton-transfer step. Label the donor of the proton, the acceptor of the proton and the electron pair forming the new bond. Audit atoms and net charge. This question asks for the electron-flow bookkeeping, not for a claim that the equilibrium lies overwhelmingly to the right.






Hint





The oxygen of hydroxide needs a new O–H bond. Where will that bonding pair come from? What happens to the methanol O–H pair when the proton leaves?









Worked check





One arrow begins at a hydroxide oxygen lone pair and ends at the methanol hydroxyl H. The second begins at the methanol O–H bond and ends on the methanol oxygen. Methanol donates H⁺ and hydroxide accepts it. The products have one carbon, five hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms in total, just as the reactants do. Net charge is −1 on each side. The relative acid pKa values, solvent and concentrations are needed to discuss the equilibrium mixture.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
text:
2. Repair a five-bonded carbon
A student adds OH⁻ to CH₃CHO by drawing a new C–O bond but retaining C=O, C–CH₃ and C–H. Draw the proposed central carbon and count its bond orders. Repair the elementary step with a second arrow. Give the charge and lone-pair count on the original carbonyl oxygen after addition. Then protonate that oxygen using water and draw the conjugate base produced from water.






Worked check





The incorrect carbon has total bond order five: C=O plus three single bonds. Move the C=O π pair to its oxygen while the new C–O bond forms. The product is CH₃CH(OH)O⁻, with the original carbonyl oxygen singly bonded, bearing three lone pairs and charge −1. Its lone pair can take H from water while the water O–H pair returns to water oxygen. Products of that transfer are CH₃CH(OH)₂ and OH⁻. Carbon remains tetravalent, and net charge remains −1.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
section: 3. A concerted substitution is not two successive reactions
text:
3. A concerted substitution is not two successive reactions
For OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻, draw the two arrows in the same step. Explain why drawing CH₃⁺ as an intermediate would propose a different mechanism. Classify OH⁻ as a nucleophile in this particular event. Is that label evidence that OH⁻ could never act as a base in another event?






Worked check





The hydroxide lone pair points to methyl carbon; the C–Br pair points to Br. Both occur in the concerted SN2 step. Drawing CH₃⁺ would replace that model with prior ionisation and a distinct intermediate, an unsuitable proposal for this methyl substitution. OH⁻ is a nucleophile because it forms a bond to carbon here. It can accept H⁺ elsewhere and then acts as a base. Identify the attacked atom instead of labelling an entire reagent permanently.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
text:
4. Read the free-energy profile



A two-step schematic free-energy profile with an intermediate between two maxima.


Redraw the profile and mark the reactants, both transition states, intermediate and products. Starting at the intermediate, show the forward and reverse activation barriers. Why is the height of the second maximum measured from the intermediate when discussing the second elementary step? Why is the horizontal axis not time?






Worked check





Maxima are transition states; the intervening minimum is an intermediate. Each elementary step’s barrier is measured from its starting minimum, not automatically from the original reactants. The reaction coordinate describes progress through changing geometry and bonding. It is not a clock; a distance along it cannot be converted into a lifetime without additional information.

title: Practice: make every arrow account for a pair
text:
5. What can a catalyst change?
Sketch reactants at one free energy and products at a lower free energy. Draw two paths joining the same endpoints with different barriers. Explain what is different about the catalysed path and what remains the same about the overall equilibrium. State where the catalyst must appear in an overall balanced description.






Worked check





A catalyst provides another pathway with lower kinetically relevant barriers. It can accelerate approach to equilibrium in both directions. It does not change the free energies of the same initial and final states or their equilibrium constant. The catalyst participates in steps but is regenerated overall; it is not consumed stoichiometrically in the net transformation.
