text:
Leave with
Three audited mechanisms, one annotated energy diagram and a two-sentence explanation distinguishing an intermediate from a transition state. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapter 3 and early chapter 6 sections; see the reading guide.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
text:
1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?
Choose a lone pair, an ordinary atom label without a specified electron pair, or a positive charge. Explain the electron accounting.






Check your answer





Start at a lone pair or a bond containing the pair being moved. A positive charge is an acceptor cue, not an electron-pair source.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
text:
2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?
OH⁻ forms a new bond to carbonyl carbon. What must happen to the C=O π pair?






Check your answer





It moves to oxygen in the same addition step. Otherwise the carbon would have total bond order five. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
3. Are two arrows two steps?
The methyl SN2 drawing has two curved arrows. Does it have two elementary steps?






Check your answer





No. Both pair movements occur in one concerted elementary step. Step counting depends on the mechanistic intermediates and barriers, not the number of arrows.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
text:
4. What distinguishes an intermediate?
On a schematic free-energy profile, is an intermediate a maximum or a minimum? How does it differ from a transition state?






Check your answer





An intermediate is a minimum between elementary steps and has a finite lifetime. A transition state lies at a barrier maximum and is not an isolable species.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
text:
5. What must a proton donor leave behind?
An alkoxide takes a proton from water. Give both products and check charge.






Check your answer





The products are an alcohol and OH⁻. Net charge starts and ends at minus one. Writing only alcohol would omit the donor-derived conjugate base.

title: Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms
section: 6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
text:
6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?
A catalyst lowers a kinetically relevant barrier. Does that change the equilibrium constant for the same reaction and conditions?






Check your answer





No. It changes the pathway and can speed approach to equilibrium in both directions. The same reactant/product endpoint free-energy difference determines the same equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Explain a concerted SN2 and a stepwise SN1 example.
Predict inversion at a reacting stereocentre.
Justify a pathway using substrate and conditions.


Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Classify the reacting carbon

Primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl bromides differ in carbon neighbours at the carbon attached to Br.Count the carbon neighbours of the carbon carrying the leaving group. Do not classify the whole molecule by total carbon count.

The highlighted region locates the reaction centre. Ask students to draw the tertiary example fully and count four bonds at its central carbon.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
section: SN2 couples bond formation and cleavage
text:
SN2 couples bond formation and cleavage

Hydroxide attacks methyl bromide from the side opposite bromine as bromide departs.One step: donor pair → carbon; C–Br bond pair → Br.
CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻.

This methyl example is deliberately simple. Hydroxide can also act as a base on suitable substrates, but methyl bromide has no beta carbon for elimination.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Backside attack inverts local geometry

A schematic chiral carbon shows its retained group arrangement inverted when Br is replaced by OH.SN2 gives inversion at the reacting tetrahedral carbon. Reassign priorities before stating a product R/S label.

The diagram uses R as a generic carbon substituent, not the R configuration descriptor. Replacing Br can change CIP priorities, so inversion does not universally mean the letter changes.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
section: Both collision partners affect the rate
text:
Both collision partners affect the rate

A schematic straight line shows initial SN2 rate proportional to nucleophile concentration at fixed substrate.For this simple model: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]. Doubling one concentration doubles initial rate when the other is fixed.

This is a mechanistic model diagram, not measured data. Rate laws are evidence for mechanisms, but a single dependence does not prove every microscopic detail.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Crowding obstructs backside approach

Substituent spheres illustrate less accessible attack at a more substituted saturated carbon.Methyl and many primary substrates are accessible to SN2. Tertiary alkyl centres strongly obstruct the required approach.

This drawing illustrates access rather than molecular dimensions. Solvent and nucleophile still matter; do not teach substrate class as the only variable.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
SN1 begins by forming ions

A tertiary C–Br bond cleaves to a tertiary carbocation and bromide.Ionisation precedes nucleophile capture. A suitable polar medium can stabilise charged species.

Show a real bond pair moving to Br. Forming a carbocation has an energy cost; students should not transfer this step to methyl or ordinary primary substrates.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Water can be a nucleophile

A water oxygen lone pair attacks a carbocation to give a protonated alcohol.A neutral nucleophile can form a new bond. Here the attacking oxygen becomes positively charged.

Count three oxygen bonds in the oxonium product. Do not let students write a neutral alcohol at this stage; that would lose an H and change the charge.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Finish the proton transfer

A second water molecule accepts H from the oxonium ion, giving alcohol and hydronium.The neutral alcohol is produced by deprotonation, not by silently deleting H⁺.

Track a spectator bromide separately if writing the whole solution reaction. All individual steps must conserve charge.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
section: A planar carbocation has two faces
text:
A planar carbocation has two faces

A planar carbocation permits nucleophilic approach from either face.An achiral medium can give both configurations. Ion-pair effects may prevent an exactly racemic product.

This is a face-access cartoon; arrows represent approaches, not a full electron-flow mechanism. Do not promise exactly 50:50 for every SN1 reaction.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Substitution is one possible outcome

A secondary alkyl bromide can follow nucleophilic substitution or beta-proton elimination.Compare substrate, leaving group, nucleophile/base, solvent and temperature. Conditions are part of the question.

We will handle elimination next. A decision should cite evidence; a colour-coded flowchart is not a substitute for explaining the elementary steps.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Which conditions support each example?
Methyl bromide + hydroxide: accessible carbon and a strong pair donor support the SN2 model.
Tertiary bromide in water: ionisation can precede water capture, with elimination competing.
Neither is a universal rule for every solvent and temperature.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Leaving-group quality matters
A departing group must accommodate its electron pair. Bromide is a plausible leaving group; OH⁻ is poor under ordinary substitution conditions.
Protonating an alcohol can allow loss as water. Draw that activation step before using it.

title: Substitution: replacing a leaving group
text:
Predict before checking
For CH₃Br + OH⁻, give the product, both curved arrows and net charge.
For (CH₃)₃CBr in water, draw ionisation, water capture and deprotonation. Name a competing outcome.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
text: Allow 90 minutes. Use a model kit or make a simple physical model for the Newman projection questions. The aim is to explain bond changes and geometry before learning product patterns.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
section: 1. Define alpha and beta for a particular substrate
text:
1. Define alpha and beta for a particular substrate
Draw 2-bromobutane, CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃. Label the carbon bearing Br as α, then label every adjacent carbon as β. Circle the β-hydrogens that could be removed in a formal elimination. Draw the constitutional alkene products.






Worked check





C2 is α; C1 and C3 are β. Removal of H from C1 can produce but-1-ene; removal from C3 can produce but-2-ene. But-2-ene has E and Z configurations because each double-bond carbon has two different substituents. But-1-ene does not, because its terminal carbon has two H atoms. This lists possible products; it does not establish their proportions under an unspecified condition.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
text:
2. Draw one E2 step
Choose a conformation of 2-bromobutane with an appropriate β-H opposite Br. Show a generic base B⁻, its lone pair and three curved arrows. Draw all products, including BH and Br⁻. Which two bonds disappear and which new bond order appears? Is there a carbocation intermediate?






Hint





Follow a closed sequence of pairs: base → H; C–H → C–C; C–Br → Br. Each arrow tail must identify a pair in the starting structure.









Worked check





The base lone pair forms B–H; the C–H pair forms the alkene π bond; the C–Br pair returns to Br. The products are the selected alkene, BH and Br⁻. C–H and C–Br are lost, while C–C changes from a single to a double bond. The concerted E2 model contains no carbocation intermediate. The net charge is −1 on each side for a B⁻ base and neutral substrate.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
section: 3. Read a Newman projection rather than memorising a shape
text:
3. Read a Newman projection rather than memorising a shape



A Newman projection with a front hydrogen and rear bromine anti at a 180-degree dihedral angle.


Identify which bonds start at the front dot and which start at the rear circle. Rebuild the depicted carbon–carbon bond with a model. Rotate one carbon by 60° and then 120° while keeping the other fixed. Does the chosen H/Br pair stay anti-periplanar? Explain why rotation changes conformation rather than configuration at an otherwise stable stereocentre.






Worked check





The selected front H and rear Br initially point in opposite directions with a dihedral angle of 180°. After a relative rotation by 60° or 120°, that particular pair is no longer anti. Other hydrogen choices may become appropriately aligned. Rotation changes torsion about the single bond without exchanging groups at a stereocentre or changing connectivity. For many flexible molecules conformational access makes several eliminations possible; constrained rings require additional care.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
section: 4. Predict and explain ionic HBr addition to propene
text:
4. Predict and explain ionic HBr addition to propene
Assume an ionic reaction without peroxides. Draw both possible carbocation connectivities that could follow protonation of CH₃CH=CH₂. Identify the more stable carbocation and complete the bromide capture step. Draw each relevant electron-flow arrow, including the H–Br bond cleavage.






Worked check





Donating the alkene π pair to H with H attaching at the terminal carbon gives the secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃; H attaching at the middle carbon would give a primary terminal carbocation. The secondary route is favoured in this selected model. The H–Br pair moves to Br, and a bromide lone pair then attacks the carbocation, giving 2-bromopropane. The explanation is relative intermediate stability in a stated mechanism, not a rule about where a written H symbol must appear in every addition reaction.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
text:
5. Contrast bromination with HBr addition
In a Br₂ addition, a bridged bromonium ion can form. Draw the ring-opening stage with bromide attacking one carbon from the opposite side and the corresponding C–Br bridge pair returning to the bridge bromine. What stereochemical relationship results between the two newly added bromines? Why should you not carry the free-carbocation HBr drawing over unchanged?






Worked check





Backside opening of the bridge gives anti addition. The bridge blocks direct same-side attack in this simple mechanism. HBr and Br₂ add different species through different intermediates, so a free carbocation mechanism is not an adequate general explanation of bromonium-mediated addition. Anti describes relative addition geometry; the exact configurations depend on the starting alkene and require drawing the actual product.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
text:
6. E1 or SN1 after ionisation?
Start with (CH₃)₃C⁺ in water. Draw one path to 2-methylpropan-2-ol and another to 2-methylpropene. Identify whether water attacks carbon or removes β-H. Explain why observing a carbocation intermediate would not by itself establish which final product is obtained.






Worked check





Water attack at carbon, then deprotonation, gives the alcohol through SN1. Water acting as a base removes β-H while the C–H pair forms C=C, giving the alkene and hydronium through E1. Both can follow ionisation; their competition depends on the conditions. Ionisation identifies an early mechanistic stage, not a unique product.

title: Practice: follow elimination and addition in space
text:
Leave with
An audited E2 drawing, an anti Newman model, and two distinct addition mechanisms. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapters 7–8; see the reading guide.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
text:
1. Can CH₃Br give an ordinary beta-elimination?
Draw the carbon skeleton before answering.






Check your answer





No. There is no beta carbon, and therefore no beta-H that could be removed to form an adjacent C=C bond.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
text:
2. How many pair arrows describe E2?
Identify the source and destination of each.






Check your answer





Three: base lone pair to beta-H; C–H bond pair into the C–C pi bond; C–leaving-group pair onto the leaving group. These describe one concerted elementary step.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
text:
3. What is anti-periplanar?
State the H–C–C–Br dihedral angle in the preferred simple anti arrangement.






Check your answer





180 degrees. The reacting C–H and C–Br bonds lie in one plane on opposite sides of the viewed C–C bond. A Newman drawing must specify front and rear bonds.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
text:
4. Which alkenes follow formal elimination from 2-bromobutane?
List constitutional possibilities and note the E/Z case.






Check your answer





But-1-ene and but-2-ene. The latter can be E or Z; but-1-ene has two H atoms at its terminal alkene carbon and cannot have E/Z configurations.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
text:
5. Why does ionic HBr addition favour 2-bromopropane from propene?
Assume no peroxides and use the supplied carbocation model.






Check your answer





Protonation giving a secondary carbocation is favoured over the alternative primary carbocation. Bromide then captures that intermediate, giving the observed connectivity in this model.

title: Self-check: Elimination and addition
section: 6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
text:
6. Why is the Br₂ route a different drawing?
Name the key bridged intermediate and the relative opening geometry.






Check your answer





A bromonium intermediate can be opened by opposite-side bromide attack, giving anti addition. A free-carbocation HBr mechanism should not be copied unchanged for this process.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Connect alcohols with aldehydes, ketones and acids.
Draw carbonyl reduction as addition then proton transfer.
Calculate a limiting amount with explicit units.


Begin with the previous unit’s electron-pair and charge audit. Ask students to predict a product or bond change before displaying the worked drawing. These slides support discussion and paper drawing; the practice page supplies further explanations.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: A primary alcohol has two oxidation targets
text:
A primary alcohol has two oxidation targets

Ethanol can be oxidised to ethanal and then ethanoic acid.Controlling conditions matters when the intended product is the aldehyde. A transformation arrow is not a complete protocol.

Use ethanol as the recurring carbon skeleton. The [O] notation summarises net oxidation and must not be treated as an elementary mechanistic atom.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: A secondary alcohol gives a ketone
text:
A secondary alcohol gives a ketone

Propan-2-ol oxidation gives propanone with the carbon skeleton retained.Identify the carbon bearing OH. Its C–H bond and O–H bond are replaced overall as the carbonyl forms.

This is a net transformation, not a universal one-step alcohol-oxidation mechanism. Different oxidants have different elementary steps.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Why is the tertiary case different?
text:
Why is the tertiary case different?

A secondary alcohol has a hydrogen on its OH-bearing carbon; a tertiary one has three carbon substituents instead.A tertiary alcohol lacks the required carbinol C–H bond for the simple alcohol → carbonyl transformation without C–C cleavage.

Do not state that tertiary alcohols can never oxidise. Harsh oxidative conditions may cleave carbon bonds; that chemistry is beyond this selected toolkit.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Use bond accounting as a check
text:
Use bond accounting as a check

The changing carbon is assigned oxidation states minus one in ethanol, plus one in ethanal and plus three in ethanoic acid.Assign C–O bond order +1 and C–H bond −1 to the carbon; C–C contributes zero. Oxidation raises the value.

For an aldehyde carbon, C=O contributes plus two and C–H minus one, giving plus one. For a carboxylic acid the three C–O bond orders give plus three.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Reduction starts with delivery of a hydride equivalent
text:
Reduction starts with delivery of a hydride equivalent

A hydride-equivalent pair forms a C–H bond at a ketone while its carbonyl pi pair moves onto oxygen.A reagent such as NaBH₄ can reduce selected aldehydes and ketones. First draw the alkoxide.

H: minus is a mechanistic shorthand for reagent delivery, not a bottle of free hydride in water. Full borate chemistry is outside the introductory scheme.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: An alkoxide still needs a proton
text:
An alkoxide still needs a proton

A separate water proton-transfer step converts the alkoxide into a neutral alcohol.Specify the proton donor. Add the conjugate base to conserve charge and H atoms.

Discuss the order: carbonyl attack, alkoxide, proton transfer. The net alcohol product does not mean all events occur at once.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Alcohol chemistry often begins with activation
text:
Alcohol chemistry often begins with activation

An alcohol can be protonated to an oxonium species from which water is a better leaving group than hydroxide.OH⁻ is generally a poor leaving group. Protonation changes what can depart.

Which reaction follows activation depends on substrate and conditions. Do not infer SN1 for every alcohol or ignore an elimination pathway.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Use evidence to test the transformation
text:
Use evidence to test the transformation

Simulated offset IR traces contrast a broad alcohol O–H region with a carbonyl absorption near 1720 inverse centimetres.A new carbonyl band supports a functional-group change. A missing broad O–H band is useful but not a complete identification.

These are synthetic schematic traces, not real spectra or a universal frequency reference. Water, concentration and overlapping bands can affect actual observations.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Choose the desired functional group first
text:
Choose the desired functional group first

Ethanol to ethanal is an oxidation, while ethanal to ethanol can use NaBH4 followed by proton donation.Say which bonds change, then justify a suitable transformation. Conditions must match the target and other functional groups.

Reagent names are examples for reasoning, not laboratory instructions. Actual lab protocols require the approved departmental directions.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
section: Calculate a maximum before an isolated yield
text:
Calculate a maximum before an isolated yield

A supplied one-to-one synthesis with 10 mmol acid and 15 mmol anhydride has a 10 mmol product maximum.Compare n/stoichiometric coefficient, not reagent masses. Use the balanced equation supplied for the actual experiment.

This task prepares the synthesis report, using aspirin data rather than an alcohol-redox reaction. Make that context switch explicit; the calculation method transfers.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
A reagent has a scope
This course uses selected transformations. Predict aldehyde/ketone reduction by NaBH₄ under suitable conditions; do not silently extend that claim to ordinary esters or amides.
Other functional groups and conditions can change the outcome.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Yield, conversion and purity differ
Isolated yield: isolated product amount / theoretical maximum.
Conversion: fraction of a starting material consumed.
Purity: fraction of the isolated material that is the desired substance.
One number cannot establish all three.

title: Alcohols and organic redox
text:
Chemical explanation before calculation
For a secondary alcohol, predict the oxidation product and explain the local bond changes.
For a balanced 1:1 synthesis with 10 and 15 mmol reagents, predict the limiting reagent before opening R.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
text: Allow 90 minutes. Colour or label the oxygen atoms so their identities remain visible through each mechanism. Use explicit proton donors and acceptors. The point is to understand the recurring pattern, not memorise every carbonyl reagent. Review the alcohol reduction for the same addition → proton-transfer pattern with a different nucleophile.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
section: 1. Partial charge is not formal charge
text:
1. Partial charge is not formal charge
Draw ethanal, CH₃CHO, with its carbonyl oxygen lone pairs. Mark the direction of bond polarity and describe the geometry at carbon. Does δ+ at carbon mean it is already a carbon atom with formal charge +1? Why can a nucleophile attack carbon rather than the electron-rich oxygen in the selected addition?






Worked check





The oxygen attracts electron density, leaving carbon partially electron-poor. Carbonyl carbon is approximately trigonal planar, with three bond directions. Both atoms have formal charge zero in the ordinary neutral Lewis structure; partial charge describes uneven electron density. The nucleophile donates a pair to the electron-poor carbon while the C=O π pair moves to oxygen, making a chemically valid four-single-bond carbon centre.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
section: 2. Base-catalysed hydration with an atom label
text:
2. Base-catalysed hydration with an atom label
Label ethanal’s oxygen A. Label the oxygen of attacking OH⁻ as B. Draw hydroxide addition and then proton transfer from water. In the hydrate, which O came from carbonyl and which from hydroxide? Why is hydroxide a catalyst in the net transformation even though a hydroxide ion appears in the first step?






Hint





After the first step, A is O⁻ and B is OH. Which species can supply H to A, and which species remains after that donor has lost H⁺?









Worked check





The first product is CH₃CH(OH-B)(O-A⁻). The B lone pair forms C–O-B while the C=O-A π pair moves onto A. Water then donates H⁺ to A and becomes OH⁻. Both A and B are OH in the hydrate CH₃CH(OH)₂, but their tracked identities remain distinct in this drawing. Hydroxide is used and regenerated overall; net hydration is ethanal + water ⇌ hydrate. The mechanism does not by itself prove that the hydrate dominates the equilibrium mixture.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
text:
3. Acid-catalysed hemiacetal formation
Start with ethanal and methanol. Label the carbonyl oxygen A and methanol oxygen B. Draw three elementary stages: protonation of A using hydronium; attack by methanol at carbon with the C=O π pair moving to A; removal of the extra proton from B by water. Give formal charges after each stage.






Worked check





Protonating A gives CH₃CH=O-AH⁺ plus water. Methanol O-B attacks carbon, giving CH₃CH(OH-A)(O-B⁺HCH₃); A now has two single bonds and is neutral, while B has three single bonds and charge +1. Water removes the B proton, giving CH₃CH(OH-A)(O-BCH₃) and hydronium. The final product is a hemiacetal: OH and OCH₃ are on the same carbon. The acid catalyst is regenerated.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
text:
4. Distinguish the product classes
For each structure, circle the carbon of interest and classify it as an aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal or acetal:

CH₃CHO
CH₃CH(OH)₂
CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃
CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂

Which difference would make it incorrect to call a hemiacetal an acetal? For the net acid-catalysed equilibrium CH₃CHO + 2 CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂ + H₂O, predict the direction favoured by adding excess water. Explain the role of acid separately from the effect of changing water concentration.






Worked check





The listed classes are aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal, respectively. A hemiacetal has one OH and one OR; an acetal has two OR groups on the same carbon. Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward aldehyde and methanol. Acid catalyses the interconversion and is regenerated; it does not change the equilibrium constant for the same net reaction under the same conditions. Converting a hemiacetal to an acetal requires additional activation, loss of water, alcohol addition and proton transfer, not a single unexplained swap.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
section: 5. Build a ring without losing an atom
text:
5. Build a ring without losing an atom
Draw the chain HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO (5-hydroxypentanal). Show how its terminal alcohol oxygen can attack the aldehyde carbon through the same chemical pattern. Draw the neutral cyclic hemiacetal after proton transfers. Count the ring atoms and compare molecular formula before and after. Is water lost in the net chain → cyclic hemiacetal transformation?






Worked check





The ring contains the attacking terminal oxygen, four methylene carbons and the original aldehyde carbon: six ring atoms. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH on that carbon. The molecular formula C₅H₁₀O₂ is unchanged; no water molecule is lost in net hemiacetal cyclisation. The oxygen that forms the ring is the original terminal alcohol oxygen. This is an organic structure argument that also helps explain why some sugars can form rings.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
text:
6. Prepare for acyl chemistry
Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Both have an electrophilic carbonyl carbon. What group is bonded to that carbon in the ester that could participate in an appropriate addition–elimination pathway? Why would treating H⁻ as an ordinary leaving group from an aldehyde be a poor explanation of addition?






Worked check





The ester has OCH₃ attached to the acyl carbon; under appropriate conditions, an oxygen-based group can depart after addition and suitable proton transfers. The aldehyde has H in that position. Hydride is not a normal leaving group in these simple aqueous carbonyl reactions, so aldehyde nucleophilic addition normally retains its H/carbon substituents. The next unit explains when and how acyl derivatives undergo substitution rather than just addition.

title: Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time
text:
Leave with
Two labelled mechanisms, four product-class assignments and an atom-conserving ring drawing. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapter 16 sections; consult the reading guide.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text: Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
text:
1. Is delta-plus the same as formal plus one?
Explain the labelled carbon in a neutral aldehyde.






Check your answer





No. Partial positive charge describes unequal electron density in the polar bond. The ordinary neutral Lewis structure assigns formal charge zero to the carbonyl carbon.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
text:
2. Which oxygen becomes O minus on initial hydroxide addition?
Label carbonyl oxygen A and hydroxide oxygen B.






Check your answer





A becomes alkoxide after receiving the carbonyl pi pair. B becomes the newly bonded OH group. The intermediate is tetrahedral and has net charge minus one.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
text:
3. Why add to protonated carbonyl under acid conditions?
Name the nucleophile in the methanol example and the purpose of O protonation.






Check your answer





Neutral methanol is the nucleophile. Protonating carbonyl oxygen increases carbonyl carbon electrophilicity. Drawing a strongly basic nucleophile freely present in excess strong acid would require reconsidering acid–base reactions.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
text:
4. Which is the hemiacetal?
Choose CH₃CH(OH)₂, CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃ or CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂.






Check your answer





CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃: one OH and one OR group at the same carbon. The first is a hydrate and the third an acetal.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
text:
5. Does a cyclic hemiacetal lose water?
Consider 5-hydroxypentanal closing by internal OH attack and proton transfers.






Check your answer





No net water is lost. The molecular formula is unchanged. Its six-membered ring contains the terminal alcohol oxygen and five carbon atoms; the original carbonyl oxygen becomes OH.

title: Self-check: Carbonyl addition
section: 6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
text:
6. How does water affect acetal equilibrium?
For aldehyde + two alcohols ⇌ acetal + water under acid catalysis, predict the direction favoured by excess water.






Check your answer





Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward aldehyde and alcohol. Acid catalyses the pathway in both directions and does not itself change the equilibrium constant.



If an answer was unexpected, return to the worked practice, repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Recognise the common acyl motif in acids, esters and amides.
Draw addition–elimination with valid electron flow and proton transfers.
Distinguish ester hydrolysis, esterification and amide formation.


Start with a drawn molecule and an explanation from the preceding unit. Ask students to predict before revealing an answer. Use the practice page for complete worked checks rather than putting dense paragraphs on slides.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
One carbonyl motif, several families

Acids, esters and amides differ in the group attached to the acyl carbon.Circle the carbonyl carbon, then name its two directly attached groups.

R denotes an organic group; OR′ distinguishes an ester from an ether. An ester has a carbonyl adjacent to the single-bond oxygen. Avoid calling every carbonyl a ketone.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
section: The first step resembles carbonyl addition
text:
The first step resembles carbonyl addition

A nucleophile donates a pair to the carbonyl carbon while the pi pair moves to oxygen.Use two arrows in the same elementary addition step.

Here Nu− is a generic anionic nucleophile and Y is the potential leaving group. This drawing illustrates unprotonated addition; acid-catalysed variants require carbonyl protonation before attack by a neutral nucleophile.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Check the tetrahedral intermediate

The former carbonyl carbon has four single bonds; oxygen carries the negative charge.The carbonyl pi bond has opened. Nu and Y are both still attached.

Ask students to count carbon bonds before calculating charge. Nu− forms a bond and becomes neutral in this generic example; negative charge is now on O. Total charge remains minus one.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
section: Collapse needs a viable leaving group
text:
Collapse needs a viable leaving group

An oxygen lone pair reforms C=O and the C–Y bond pair moves onto Y.These arrows describe one elimination step.

Y must be able to leave under the reaction conditions. Hydroxide or alkoxide may need protonation in acidic mechanisms. Do not expel H− or an ordinary alkyl carbanion from an aldehyde/ketone simply to make a substitution.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Identify the net substitution

The carbonyl is retained while Y is replaced by Nu.Addition and elimination are separate mechanistic events; the net equation hides the intermediate.

Compare with the previous carbonyl-addition lesson: ordinary aldehydes and ketones typically give addition products because they lack a suitable leaving group. No free acyl carbocation is required here.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Esterification is an equilibrium

Ethanoic acid and ethanol can form ethyl ethanoate and water under acid catalysis.The catalyst is regenerated; water removal or excess reactant can shift the equilibrium.

Have students trace the alcohol oxygen into the ester using a label. At this level show the required proton transfers without implying that an unprotonated OH group simply leaves as OH− in an acidic mechanism.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Base-promoted hydrolysis gives carboxylate

Hydroxide hydrolysis ultimately gives carboxylate and alcohol.An acid work-up is needed if the intended isolated form is the neutral carboxylic acid.

Addition then collapse initially gives acid and alkoxide in the simplest model. The subsequent acid–base reaction strongly favours carboxylate and alcohol. Hydroxide is consumed overall, so base is not merely a regenerated catalyst in saponification.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Why an amide is different

Amide nitrogen donates into the carbonyl, giving partial C–N double-bond character.Use resonance to explain restricted rotation and reduced nitrogen basicity.

These are contributors to one molecule, not two isomers. The charge-separated contributor has O− and N+, preserving net neutrality. Under comparable conditions ordinary amides are less reactive toward acyl substitution than esters.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
section: Mixing acid and amine does not suffice
text:
Mixing acid and amine does not suffice

Acid and amine initially undergo proton transfer to give an ammonium carboxylate.Making an amide requires suitable activation or conditions.

This corrects a frequent biologically motivated misconception: peptide bonds do not form rapidly just because two amino acids encounter each other in water. Later biochemistry explains how activation and enzymes enable coupling.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Recognise the motif in biology

Lipid esters and peptide amides contain the same acyl-carbon framework.The leaving group, activation and environment change the chemistry; the electron bookkeeping remains useful.

No metabolic pathways are prerequisites here. Ask only which bond is ester-like or amide-like and where a nucleophile would initially attack.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
Work one example on paper
For CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + OH⁻, draw the tetrahedral intermediate, its collapse, and the final acid–base step. Label the alcohol product and distinguish the reaction mixture from its acid-worked-up form.

Allow independent thinking, then compare in pairs. Ask students to defend each atom, charge or assignment. Show the worked check only after a first attempt.

title: Acyl chemistry: esters, amides and their reactions
text:
A common mistake to repair
A mechanism that expels OH⁻ from an acid-protonated intermediate without checking protonation state usually skips an essential proton transfer. Check every oxygen charge after each step.
Explain the correction using a drawing or a specific observation.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
text: Allow 60–75 minutes. Draw structures rather than relying on a nitrogen label. You need formal charges, pKa comparisons and resonance. No metabolic knowledge is assumed.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
text:
1. Classify and protonate
Draw methylamine, dimethylamine and trimethylamine with their nitrogen lone pairs. Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary. Protonate each once, showing an explicit acid H–A as donor and the corresponding A⁻ product. Count bonds and formal charge on every nitrogen before and after the change.






Hint





A neutral nitrogen with three ordinary single bonds has one lone pair. After using that pair to bind H, it has four bonds and a positive charge.









Worked check





CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH and (CH₃)₃N have one, two and three carbon substituents on N, respectively. Their conjugate acids are CH₃NH₃⁺, (CH₃)₂NH₂⁺ and (CH₃)₃NH⁺. Draw N pair → H and H–A bond → A in the same proton transfer. A tertiary amine is neutral before protonation; it is not the same as a quaternary ammonium ion bearing four carbon substituents.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
section: 2. Compare base strength using supplied data
text:
2. Compare base strength using supplied data
Use approximate aqueous conjugate-acid pKa values: ethylammonium 10.7 and anilinium 4.6. Which corresponding neutral amine is the stronger base? Estimate the equilibrium constant for anilinium + ethylamine ⇌ aniline + ethylammonium. Explain the structural difference without asserting that basicity determines all nucleophilic reaction rates.






Worked check





Ethylamine is the stronger base because its conjugate acid is weaker (larger pKa). The estimated constant is 10^(10.7 − 4.6), about 1.26 × 10⁶ toward aniline and ethylammonium. Aniline can delocalise its N pair into the aromatic ring. Basicity concerns an equilibrium; nucleophilicity concerns a reaction rate and also depends on substrate, solvent and other factors.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
text:
3. Count the aromatic electrons carefully
Draw benzene, cyclohexane, pyridine and pyrrole. For each state whether a continuous cyclic pi system exists. In pyridine and pyrrole identify whether the nitrogen lone pair contributes to the aromatic sextet. Predict which nitrogen is more readily protonated under comparable ordinary conditions.






Worked check





Benzene has six pi electrons and is aromatic. Cyclohexane lacks continuous conjugation and is nonaromatic. Pyridine N contributes one electron to its pi system; its separate lone pair is available to bind a proton while retaining aromaticity. Pyrrole uses its pair in the six-electron aromatic system, making ordinary N protonation much less favourable. Pyridine is therefore the more basic nitrogen in this comparison. “Both contain a ring N” misses the orbital difference.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
text:
4. Draw glycine across pH
Use supplied approximate pKa values 2.3 for the carboxyl group and 9.6 for the ammonium group. Draw the dominant form at pH 1, 6 and 12; label every formal charge and calculate the net charge. Explain what changes around each pKa, rather than implying an abrupt switch between pure forms.






Hint





At pH well below a site’s pKa, its protonated form predominates. At pH well above it, its deprotonated form predominates. Apply this separately to the two sites.









Worked check





At pH 1: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH, net +1. At pH 6: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻, net zero. At pH 12: H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻, net −1. The middle form is a zwitterion because it contains both positive and negative formal charges. Around each pKa adjacent forms coexist; these drawings describe dominant forms sufficiently away from the transition, not an all-or-nothing population rule.

title: Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?
text:
5. Amine versus peptide nitrogen
Place CH₃CH₂NH₂ and CH₃CONH₂ side by side. Draw the amide resonance contributors and explain why assigning “amine-like basicity” to every nitrogen in a protein would fail. Give one structural feature you would inspect before predicting the nitrogen’s behaviour.






Worked check





The amide N pair is delocalised into a neighbouring carbonyl; the simple amine pair is not. Peptide nitrogens are amide nitrogens. Inspect direct attachment to C=O, aromaticity and conjugation before applying a simple alkylamine model.



See the reading guide for selected Solomons chapters 14 and 20 and an open textbook reference.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
1. Is a tertiary amine charged?
Trimethylamine has three methyl groups on N. State its charge before and after accepting one proton.






Check your answer





Neutral (CH₃)₃N has three N–C bonds and one lone pair. Its conjugate acid (CH₃)₃NH⁺ has four bonds and charge +1.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
text:
2. Which pKa belongs in a basicity comparison?
Conjugate-acid pKa values are 10.7 for ethylammonium and 4.6 for anilinium. Which neutral base is stronger in comparable aqueous conditions?






Check your answer





Ethylamine. Its conjugate acid is the weaker acid with larger pKa. Basicity is an equilibrium property and is not a universal nucleophilic-rate ranking.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
text:
3. Is cyclohexane aromatic?
It is a six-membered ring. Explain why this is insufficient.






Check your answer





It has no continuous cyclic p-orbital network. It is nonaromatic; being cyclic does not imply aromaticity or antiaromaticity.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
text:
4. Which nitrogen pair is in the sextet?
Compare pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen lone pairs.






Check your answer





The pyridine lone pair lies outside its aromatic pi system. The pyrrole pair supplies two of the six aromatic pi electrons, making ordinary N protonation much less favourable.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 5. Does net zero mean no charge?
text:
5. Does net zero mean no charge?
Draw glycine in its predominant form near pH 6 with supplied pKa values 2.3 and 9.6.






Check your answer





H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ has N charge +1 and carboxylate charge −1, giving net zero. It is a zwitterion, not an entirely uncharged molecule.

title: Self-check: nitrogen and aromaticity
section: 6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
text:
6. Is peptide nitrogen a simple amine?
Identify the neighbouring structural feature that changes its electron availability.






Check your answer





Peptide nitrogen is directly attached to a carbonyl as part of an amide. Its pair delocalises into C=O, unlike the pair in a simple alkylamine.

title: Structure from spectra
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Use formula, IR and simple one-dimensional NMR together.
Assign simple integrations and first-order splitting patterns.
Reject a candidate with an explicit contradiction rather than visual resemblance.


Start with a drawn molecule and an explanation from the preceding unit. Ask students to predict before revealing an answer. Use the practice page for complete worked checks rather than putting dense paragraphs on slides.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Start with the formula

Ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid both fit C₄H₈O₂ and one degree of unsaturation.One formula can describe several connectivities.

The formula calculation assumes an ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule. A degree of unsaturation can be a ring or a double bond; oxygen does not affect the simple count.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
IR reports bond environments

A simulated ester spectrum shows strong C=O absorption and no broad O–H band.Band position and pattern constrain functional groups; IR alone does not uniquely establish connectivity.

All traces in this unit are deliberately simulated teaching data. Real peak positions and shapes vary with solvent, phase, concentration and structure. Present carbonyl bands as regions, not exact identity barcodes.

title: Structure from spectra
section: Ask what a competing candidate predicts
text:
Ask what a competing candidate predicts

A simulated acid spectrum includes a very broad acid O–H region along with C=O.A missing predicted feature can challenge the acid candidate when data quality is adequate.

Do not make absence stronger than the experiment supports. A poor or incomplete spectrum can hide a feature; ask whether the region was measured and whether the signal is detectable.

title: Structure from spectra
section: An alcohol gives a different pattern
text:
An alcohol gives a different pattern

A simulated alcohol trace has broad O–H absorption but lacks C=O.Combine presence and absence rather than matching one isolated dip.

The teaching comparison separates three clear motifs. Hydrogen bonding affects O–H width; a free OH in a different environment need not have this broad shape.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Read the proton NMR evidence

U1 has 4.12 ppm quartet integrating to 2H, 2.05 ppm singlet to 3H and 1.25 ppm triplet to 3H.The integrals total eight hydrogens, consistent with the supplied formula.

These are illustrative values and a schematic spectrum. Peak height is not integration; the printed integrals are independent supplied information. State a first-order, rapidly averaging solution assumption.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Connect a quartet and triplet

A simple O–CH₂–CH₃ group gives a CH₂ quartet and CH₃ triplet with 2:3 integration.Use the n + 1 rule only for the simple neighbouring equivalent-H cases in this course.

Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other. OH splitting and exchange can differ; do not extend this shortcut to all spectra or strongly coupled systems.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Account for the singlet too

The acetyl methyl has no adjacent carbon-bound hydrogen across the carbonyl carbon.Its three hydrogens can appear as a singlet near 2 ppm.

Do not count the two hydrogens on the distant O–CH₂ as adjacent neighbours of this methyl. We ignore small long-range couplings in this introductory model.

title: Structure from spectra
section: Use carbon NMR as another check
text:
Use carbon NMR as another check

Four illustrative carbon resonances occur at 14, 21, 60 and 171 ppm.Assign alkyl carbon, acetyl methyl, O–CH₂ and ester carbonyl environments.

The common proton-decoupled carbon spectrum gives approximate environment information. Signal heights are not reliable carbon counts, and chemically equivalent carbons can share one signal.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Make a complete assignment

Ethyl ethanoate accounts for the IR carbonyl and all three proton environments.An assignment should explain the whole supplied dataset.

Have students annotate a structure with the actual numbers and integrals. This prevents a plausible guess from replacing an evidence-based assignment.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Try to falsify the candidate

Butanoic acid predicts acid O–H and different proton environments.Its expected pattern conflicts with several features of U1.

One inconsistency may be explained by experimental conditions; multiple independent inconsistencies make rejection stronger. Spectra narrow candidates, but need not exclude every imaginable structure with absolute certainty.

title: Structure from spectra
text:
Work one example on paper
For U1 (C₄H₈O₂), assign each supplied proton and carbon NMR signal to ethyl ethanoate. Then state two observations that reject butanoic acid, without using the sample filename as evidence.

Allow independent thinking, then compare in pairs. Ask students to defend each atom, charge or assignment. Show the worked check only after a first attempt.

A tall NMR line is not a large integral. Integration concerns area; the schematic drawings provide the integral values separately.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
text: Allow 75 minutes for the chemistry questions, plus about 50 minutes for your Rmd results section. This uses simulated teaching data, not an approved experimental procedure. See practical work and reporting for the record and report workflow.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
section: 1. A short route, with a reason for each step
text:
1. A short route, with a reason for each step
Propose a route from ethanol to ethyl ethanoate using ethanoic acid as an intermediate. State the functional-group change at each step and where an additional ethanol portion is required. Why would a procedure designed to isolate ethanal not automatically be suitable for the acid target?






Worked route





Oxidise an ethanol portion to ethanoic acid under appropriate oxidation conditions, then combine the acid with a separate ethanol portion in an acid-catalysed esterification equilibrium. The first transformation is alcohol oxidation; the second is acyl substitution. Conditions that stop at or isolate ethanal serve a different target from conditions permitting further oxidation to the acid. Reagent identity and work-up would need an approved protocol before carrying this out experimentally.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
text:
2. A balanced aspirin amount table
The teaching reaction is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic acid, with 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry. Supplied masses and molar masses:



Reagent
Mass / g
Molar mass / (g mol⁻¹)




Salicylic acid
1.3812
138.12


Acetic anhydride
1.53135
102.09



Calculate amount as mass/molar mass. Compare amount divided by stoichiometric coefficient to identify the limiting reagent. Aspirin molar mass is 180.16 g/mol. Predict the theoretical product mass before using the isolated mass.






Hint





Dividing g by g/mol gives mol. One mmol is 0.001 mol. A larger mass does not necessarily indicate an excess reagent; use the balanced reaction.









Worked calculation





Salicylic acid: 0.01000 mol = 10.00 mmol. Acetic anhydride: 0.01500 mol = 15.00 mmol. With coefficients of one, salicylic acid limits product to 0.01000 mol. The theoretical mass is 0.01000 × 180.16 = 1.8016 g. This is a stoichiometric upper bound under the assumed desired reaction, not evidence that all of the starting material actually reacted.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
text:
3. Isolated yield is not purity
The isolated material weighs 1.20 g. Calculate apparent isolated yield as 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g. Name two ways this mass could overstate the true mass of product. Would a yield below 100% establish purity?






Worked check





Yield is about 66.6%. Residual solvent, water, starting material or other impurities could add to the measured mass. A value below 100% does not prove purity: impure material can still weigh less than the theoretical product. Conversion measures starting-material consumption; selectivity measures how much of reacted material follows the desired route. Neither is established solely by this isolated mass.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
text:
4. A TLC observation with limits
The solvent front travels 5.0 cm. Starting-material reference and product reference travel 1.2 and 3.2 cm respectively. The crude sample has two spots at those same distances under the same conditions. Calculate both Rf values and give a restrained interpretation. Explain why one spot from the isolate would still not uniquely identify it or prove purity.






Worked check





Rf values are 0.24 and 0.64. The crude contains at least two detected components under these conditions, with spots consistent with the references. Different compounds can co-migrate, and some components can be invisible to the detection method. Compare spectra and use other suitable evidence rather than treating Rf as a unique identity code.

title: Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain
section: 5. Rmd task: results that update when a mass changes
text:
5. Rmd task: results that update when a mass changes
In the student project, save a results section containing the amount table, limiting-reagent reasoning, theoretical mass and isolated yield. Reuse code from the report guide or adapt this transparent calculation:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
theoretical_product_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_mass_g <- theoretical_product_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
knitr::kable(amounts)
isolated_yield_percent
The amounts.csv table contains the two starting reagents. If adding product or solvent rows later, select the relevant starting reagents before min(). Inspect the table and check the units. Write the numerical yield using inline R in the report, not by typing a second independent copy of the number. Add your TLC table and an interpretation distinguishing evidence for reaction, identity and purity. Change the isolated mass to 1.10 g, predict the direction of change, and Knit again before restoring the original teaching value.






Reproducibility check





At 1.10 g the apparent isolated yield becomes about 61.1%. Every dependent result should change when knitted. If a copied number remains 66.6%, it is no longer linked to the saved calculation. Correctness also requires the right stoichiometry and trustworthy primary observations; automatic updating alone cannot supply either.



Finish with two sentences stating what the observations support and what remains uncertain. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapters 8, 12 and 17; see the reading guide.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text: Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
1. Which reagent limits?
A 1:1 reaction uses 10.0 mmol A and 15.0 mmol B. How much product can form stoichiometrically?






Check your answer





At most 10.0 mmol of the stated 1:1 product under the assumed desired transformation. A limits; leftover B does not increase that maximum.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
2. What if coefficients differ?
For 2A + B → P, with 10 mmol A and 8 mmol B, identify the limiting reagent and maximum P amount.






Check your answer





Compare 10/2 = 5 mmol with 8/1 = 8 mmol. A limits and at most 5 mmol P forms. Comparing amounts without coefficients would be misleading.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
3. What does 1.20 g mean?
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. Calculate apparent isolated yield and state its purity assumption.






Check your answer





100×1.20/1.8016 ≈ 66.6%. The calculation treats isolated mass as product mass; impurities or solvent can bias that assumption.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
4. What is Rf?
A spot travels 3.2 cm and solvent front 5.0 cm from the origin. Calculate Rf and give units.






Check your answer





Rf = 0.64, dimensionless. Both distances must be measured from the same origin; the ratio depends on separation conditions.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
5. Does one spot establish purity?
Give two reasons a mixture might show only one TLC spot.






Check your answer





Distinct compounds can co-migrate, and a component may not be detected by the chosen visualisation. One spot under one condition does not uniquely identify or prove purity.

title: Self-check: synthesis and evidence
text:
6. What should change after Knit?
You change isolated mass from 1.20 to 1.10 g. Predict the effect and the approximate new yield.






Check your answer





The yield decreases to about 61.1%. Tables and inline computed values should update from saved inputs; manually copied numbers may not.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: What will you be able to explain?
text:
What will you be able to explain?

Transfer structure and electron-flow reasoning to an unfamiliar molecule.
Build an explanation from several independent observations.
Communicate a defensible chemical claim with explicit limits.


Start with a drawn molecule and an explanation from the preceding unit. Ask students to predict before revealing an answer. Use the practice page for complete worked checks rather than putting dense paragraphs on slides.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Read the molecule before predicting reactions
text:
Read the molecule before predicting reactions

Lactic acid has a secondary alcohol, a carboxylic acid and one tetrahedral stereocentre.Predict which site is relevant before naming a reaction.

Supply the biological context: lactate is encountered in metabolism, but no pathway knowledge is required. Each prediction here follows from its functional groups.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Preserve connectivity in a stereochemical comparison
text:
Preserve connectivity in a stereochemical comparison

The two drawings have the same connectivity and opposite tetrahedral arrangements.A rotation of a drawing must preserve its configuration; a mirror-related configuration does not.

Ask students to use a model or tracing paper. If assigning R/S, priorities at the centre are OH > COOH > CH3 > H. Optical rotation sign is not inferred from R/S.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Separate acid–base change from configurational change
text:
Separate acid–base change from configurational change

Hydroxide removes the carboxyl proton to form lactate and water.This drawn proton transfer neither breaks a bond at the stereocentre nor inverts it.

This is a specific chemical transformation under the stated simple conditions, not a promise that no other conditions could racemise a chiral acid.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Oxidation can remove a stereocentre

Oxidising the secondary alcohol gives pyruvic acid with a planar ketone carbon.Track which carbon changes bonding and geometry.

Do not label the ketone carbon R or S. The transformation is a functional-group example; enzyme identity or metabolic details are not prerequisites.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Acyl substitution acts at a different site
text:
Acyl substitution acts at a different site

The target ester forms at the carboxylic acid group; the secondary OH remains in the chosen product.Recognise the target bond before proposing a mechanism.

Lactic acid has two oxygen-containing functions and can have competing chemistry. The displayed transformation specifies a target and is not a complete selectivity guarantee or executable procedure.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Choose addition or substitution from structure
text:
Choose addition or substitution from structure

Aldehyde/ketone addition and acyl substitution both begin at carbonyl carbon.A viable leaving group allows the carbonyl to reform during substitution.

Require a drawn intermediate, not only the words addition/elimination. Watch for students drawing five bonds at carbon or eliminating an ordinary carbon substituent.

title: Putting the chemistry together
section: Revisit formal charge in a biological-looking molecule
text:
Revisit formal charge in a biological-looking molecule

Alanine can have protonated amine and carboxylate at the same time.Count each formal charge before stating the net charge.

Net zero does not imply nonpolar. A zwitterion contains separated charges and can interact strongly with water; physical behaviour still depends on environment and structure.

title: Putting the chemistry together
text:
Require the observations to agree

Formula, carbonyl evidence and an ethyl/acetyl proton pattern support an ester candidate.Explain how each observation tests a different feature of the proposal.

Avoid circular reasoning: the filename or expected lab target cannot serve as spectral proof. Students should explicitly compare at least one alternative.

A plausible yield does not prove identity

A high apparent mass-based yield can coexist with contradictory IR or NMR evidence.Investigate the discrepancy before concluding that synthesis succeeded.

The 94.4% value is calculated from 1.70/1.8016×100. It is not an assessed purity, and unreacted material or residual solvent may contribute to mass.

text:
Write an explanation another chemist can inspect

A claim is linked to observations, a chemical reason and remaining uncertainty.State what further observation would most directly test the remaining alternative.

A strong report can reject its original hypothesis when the evidence contradicts it. Reproducibility includes saved data and code, but scientific reasoning must also be explicit.

A student calls an isolate pure product because the apparent yield is 94% and TLC has one spot. Their IR contains an unexpected broad O–H band and NMR contains an extra major set of signals. Write a supported interpretation and propose the next observation.

Allow independent thinking, then compare in pairs. Ask students to defend each atom, charge or assignment. Show the worked check only after a first attempt.
